title: F01 - fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
02 - Explore component distributions
Before choosing response distributions, we’ll look at how much the observed loads vary and how often a component is absent. The summaries below give means, spread, quantiles, zero counts, and missingness by phase, component, and treatment. Site, block, and corner counts show the available replication. These are raw descriptions of the transects; adjustment for the sampling hierarchy comes with the models later.


Code
# f01-02-explore-components
if (recompute) {
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  components <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-components-transect.rds"))
  paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds"))

  add_design_groups <- function(data) {
    data |>
      mutate(
        block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
        design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
      )
  }

  component_data <- components |>
    mutate(component = as.character(component)) |>
    add_design_groups()

  component_summary <- component_data |>
    summarise(
      n_transects = n(),
      n_sites = n_distinct(site),
      n_blocks = n_distinct(block),
      n_corners = n_distinct(design_corner),
      n_zero = sum(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      prop_zero = mean(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(load_mgha)),
      mean_mgha = mean(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_mgha = sd(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      variance_mgha = var(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      cv = if_else(mean_mgha > 0, sd_mgha / mean_mgha, NA_real_),
      min_mgha = min(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      q25_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
      median_mgha = median(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      q75_mgha = quantile(load_mgha, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
      max_mgha = max(load_mgha, na.rm = TRUE),
      .by = c("phase", "component", "treatment")
    ) |>
    arrange(phase, component, treatment)
  write_csv(
    component_summary,
    file.path(paths$data, "fuel-component-exploration-summary.csv")
  )
}

  "outputs/fuel/data/fuel-component-exploration-summary.csv"

Observed zeros help us decide which components need a model for absence as well as positive load. We’ll translate that information and any missingness into a table of proposed families and submodels, retaining the design random intercepts. This table is a guide to the fitting stage; it contains no fitted effects or model comparisons yet.


Code
# f01-02-component-candidates
if (recompute) {
  component_candidates <- component_data |>
    summarise(
      n_zero = sum(load_mgha == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_transects = n(),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(load_mgha)),
      .by = c("phase", "component")
    ) |>
    mutate(
      response_type = "nonnegative continuous load",
      fixed_effects = "treatment",
      random_effects = "(1 | site) + (1 | site:treatment) + (1 | site:treatment:corner)",
      conditional_family = if_else(
        n_zero > 0,
        "ziGamma(link = log)",
        "Gamma(link = log)"
      ),
      zero_inflation_candidates = if_else(
        n_zero > 0,
        "~1; consider ~treatment only if zero-process diagnostics and replication support it",
        "none unless later diagnostics identify a structural-zero process"
      ),
      dispersion_candidates = "~1 first; compare ~treatment only if residual dispersion diagnostics support it",
      status = if_else(
        n_missing > 0,
        "candidate specifications only; resolve missing values before model fitting",
        "candidate specifications only; no model fitted"
      )
    ) |>
    arrange(phase, component)
  write_csv(
    component_candidates,
    file.path(paths$manifests, "fuel-component-model-candidates.csv")
  )
}

title: F01 - fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
03 - Fit phase-component candidates
We’ll now ask whether treatment differences in each component can be described with a common residual dispersion, or whether dispersion also needs to vary by treatment. Positive loads use Gamma models with a log link; components with zeros also get a zero submodel, with treatment-specific zero probabilities considered when there are at least eight zeros. The code defines these candidates and retains the additional site and dispersion alternatives for post-PCT 100-hour fuel.


Code
# f01-03-fit-phase-components
if (recompute) {
  # Preserve the fresh-Rscript RNG boundary of this historical fitting stage.
  # DHARMa 0.5.0 consumes an extra draw when .Random.seed is initially absent.
  if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
    rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
  }
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  # Reuse the fitting functions defined above.

  library(dplyr)
  library(purrr)
  library(readr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
  components <- readRDS(file.path(
    paths$data,
    "fuel-components-transect.rds"
  )) |>
    mutate(
      component = as.character(component),
      block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
      design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE)
    )

  design_formula <- load_mgha ~ treatment +
    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner)

  fit_component_candidates <- function(data, phase_value, component_value) {
    model_data <- data |>
      filter(
        .data$phase == .env$phase_value,
        .data$component == .env$component_value,
        !is.na(load_mgha)
      )
    zero_count <- sum(model_data$load_mgha == 0)
    prefix <- paste(phase_value, component_value, sep = "_")

    candidates <- list()
    if (zero_count > 0) {
      candidates[["base"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~1,
        dispformula = ~1
      )
      candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~1,
        dispformula = ~treatment
      )
      if (zero_count >= 8) {
        candidates[["zi_treatment"]] <- list(
          family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
          family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
          ziformula = ~treatment,
          dispformula = ~1
        )
      }
    } else {
      candidates[["base"]] <- list(
        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
        ziformula = ~0,
        dispformula = ~1
      )
      candidates[["disp_treatment"]] <- list(
        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
        ziformula = ~0,
        dispformula = ~treatment
      )
    }

    # The thesis used site plus treatment in both the zero and dispersion
    # submodels for post-PCT 100-hour fuels. Retain that candidate and add one
    # deliberately more complex site-by-treatment dispersion sensitivity check.
    if (phase_value == "postpct" && component_value == "hundhr") {
      candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~ treatment + site,
        dispformula = ~ treatment + site
      )
      candidates[["zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site_interaction"]] <- list(
        family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
        family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
        ziformula = ~ treatment + site,
        dispformula = ~ treatment * site
      )
    }

    imap_dfr(candidates, function(candidate, candidate_name) {
      fit_and_diagnose(
        simulation_n = 1000,
        simulation_seed = 20260918,
        model_id = paste(prefix, candidate_name, sep = "_"),
        response = component_value,
        analysis = paste(phase_value, "phase-specific component", sep = ": "),
        data = model_data,
        formula = design_formula,
        family = candidate$family,
        family_label = candidate$family_label,
        ziformula = candidate$ziformula,
        dispformula = candidate$dispformula,
        paths = paths
      )
    })
  }
}


We’ll apply those candidates to each component–phase dataset and collect every attempt in the register below. Convergence fields and DHARMa tests, based on 1,000 unconditional simulations with seed 20260918, help identify fits needing follow-up before we use their treatment estimates.


Code
# f01-03-fit-register
if (recompute) {
  registry <- components |>
    distinct(phase, component) |>
    arrange(phase, component) |>
    pmap_dfr(function(phase, component) {
      fit_component_candidates(components, phase, component)
    })

  write_csv(
    registry,
    file.path(paths$manifests, "phase-component-model-registry.csv")
  )
}

title: F01 - fuel-component separation and model exploration
text:
04 - Fit matched woody candidates
Without a defensible post-PCT slash-depth conversion, the change in standing woody load offers one way to explore PCT’s potential contribution to surface fuels. We’ll compare a model of the paired differences with a joint model of the two phases. Woody loads are nonnegative, include zeros, and can be strongly right-skewed. A difference between two such loads can be negative, zero, or positive, with a distribution unlike either phase alone. Modeling the loads jointly respects their original scale and supplies both phase estimates. Modeling the observed differences directly asks whether a simpler change response gives a defensible account of the same paired data. These alternatives test different distributional and variance assumptions; they do not change the definition of woody reduction.
For transect \(i\), the observed signed difference is \(d_i = y_{i,\mathrm{pre}} - y_{i,\mathrm{post}}\). Positive values indicate less standing woody vegetation after PCT; negative values indicate more. Here, “signed-difference model” means fitting \(d_i\) directly, while “contrast from the joint phase model” means subtracting its two fitted response-scale means. Both yield signed changes in Mg/ha; a contrast is a derived quantity, not a separate response family.








Feature
Joint phase model and derived contrast
Direct signed-difference model




Response
Two woody loads per matched transect, one per phase.
One observed pre-minus-post difference per matched transect.


Treatment effects
phase * treatment allows phase change to vary by treatment.
treatment allows the difference to vary by treatment.


Distribution
A zero probability plus a Gamma distribution for positive loads, with a log link.
Gaussian or Student-t with an identity link, allowing either sign.


Pairing and design
Site, block, and corner random intercepts, plus a shared transect intercept linking the two phases.
Pairing is already used in the subtraction; site, block, and corner random intercepts retain clustering among differences.


Available estimates
Pre- and post-PCT mean loads and their covariance-aware difference.
Treatment-specific differences; the two phase means cannot be recovered from differences alone.



For the joint model, RD04 derives \(\Delta_t = \mu_{\mathrm{pre},t} - \mu_{\mathrm{post},t}\) from means that include the zero probability and integrate over the fitted random effects, with equal study-site weights. Exponentiating a phase contrast on the log scale would instead give a ratio in the positive-load submodel. The uncertainty of the response-scale difference retains the covariance between the estimated phase means: \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\Delta_t) =
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{pre},t}) +
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{post},t}) -
2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{pre},t},\hat\mu_{\mathrm{post},t})\). The direct model represents paired change through the distribution of \(d_i\) itself. Although \(E(Y_{\mathrm{pre}}-Y_{\mathrm{post}}) =
E(Y_{\mathrm{pre}})-E(Y_{\mathrm{post}})\) when the means exist, separately fitted models need not give identical estimates or intervals because their assumptions and use of the phase information differ.
The three joint candidates use a common zero probability and dispersion, a phase-specific zero probability, or phase-specific dispersion. These distinguish changes in the frequency of absent woody vegetation from changes in the spread of positive loads. The six direct candidates use Gaussian errors with common or treatment-specific dispersion, or Student-t errors with common, treatment, additive treatment-plus-site, or treatment-by-site dispersion. Student-t provides heavier tails for unusually large changes; the dispersion alternatives assess whether residual spread differs among treatments and sites. No zero-inflation submodel is used for the signed response: a zero difference means equal phase loads, not necessarily absent woody vegetation. The family and submodel definitions follow the glmmTMB family documentation and fitting documentation.
The current saved fits use 234 phase-load observations or 117 paired differences. Their likelihoods describe different responses, so AIC is compared within each approach, not across the two approaches, following the same-data requirement for AIC. Convergence and residual checks still determine what needs follow-up. RD04 uses the joint model so its displayed woody change agrees with its phase means; the direct models remain sensitivity candidates. Neither approach establishes a causal PCT effect or measures slash production directly.
The cell below fits both candidate sets and brings all nine attempts into one register. We’ll use its convergence and residual fields to assess the alternatives alongside AIC within each approach. Diagnostics use 1,000 unconditional DHARMa simulations with seed 20260918; recompute reads saved models, refit replaces them, and an ordinary render shows the saved register.


Code
# f01-04-fit-woody-pct-models
if (recompute) {
  # This stage formerly started in a separate Rscript process. Restore its empty
  # initial RNG state; the diagnostic seed and unconditional simulations are unchanged.
  if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
    rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
  }
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  # Reuse the fitting functions defined above.

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(tidyr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  output_paths <- model_output_paths(paths)
  paired <- readRDS(file.path(paths$data, "fuel-paired-transect.rds")) |>
    mutate(
      block = interaction(site, treatment, drop = TRUE),
      design_corner = interaction(site, treatment, corner, drop = TRUE),
      transect_id = interaction(site, treatment, corner, azi, drop = TRUE)
    )

  woody_long <- paired |>
    select(
      site,
      treatment,
      corner,
      azi,
      block,
      design_corner,
      transect_id,
      woody_vegetation_prepct,
      woody_vegetation_postpct
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("woody_vegetation_"),
      names_to = "phase",
      names_prefix = "woody_vegetation_",
      values_to = "load_mgha"
    ) |>
    mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("prepct", "postpct")))

  phase_formula <- load_mgha ~ phase *
    treatment +
    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner) +
    (1 | transect_id)

  # Model the paired phase loads; RD04 derives their response-scale contrast.
  phase_registry <- bind_rows(
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_zi1_disp1",
      response = "woody vegetation load",
      analysis = "matched repeated-measures phase model",
      data = woody_long,
      formula = phase_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
      family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ziformula = ~1,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_ziphase_disp1",
      response = "woody vegetation load",
      analysis = "matched repeated-measures phase model",
      data = woody_long,
      formula = phase_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
      family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ziformula = ~phase,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_phase_zigamma_zi1_dispphase",
      response = "woody vegetation load",
      analysis = "matched repeated-measures phase model",
      data = woody_long,
      formula = phase_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::ziGamma(link = "log"),
      family_label = "ziGamma(link = log)",
      ziformula = ~1,
      dispformula = ~phase,
      paths = paths
    )
  )

  # Model each transect's observed signed difference directly.
  delta_formula <- woody_standing_reduction_mgha ~ treatment +
    (1 | site) +
    (1 | block) +
    (1 | design_corner)

  delta_registry <- bind_rows(
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_gaussian",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = gaussian(),
      family_label = "Gaussian(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_gaussian_disp_treatment",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = gaussian(),
      family_label = "Gaussian(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~treatment,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::t_family(),
      family_label = "Student-t(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~1,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t_disp_treatment",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::t_family(),
      family_label = "Student-t(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~treatment,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t_disp_treatment_site",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",
      analysis = "signed matched pre-minus-post contrast",
      data = paired,
      formula = delta_formula,
      family = glmmTMB::t_family(),
      family_label = "Student-t(identity)",
      ziformula = ~0,
      dispformula = ~ treatment + site,
      paths = paths
    ),
    fit_and_diagnose(
      simulation_n = 1000,
      simulation_seed = 20260918,
      model_id = "woody_delta_student_t_disp_treatment_site_interaction",
      response = "woody standing-vegetation reduction",

  write_csv(
    bind_rows(phase_registry, delta_registry),

text:
05 - Evaluate provisional model leaders
With the candidate fits assembled, we can ask which has the strongest relative support within each response and analysis group. The comparison below ranks AIC and shows the distance from the leader while retaining convergence and residual evidence. These rankings narrow the review; they do not settle whether the model assumptions are suitable for the study question.


Code
# f01-05-evaluate-and-select-models
if (recompute) {
  publication_root <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/")
  paths_common <- publication_paths(publication_root)

  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)

  paths <- publication_fuel_paths(publication_root)
  registry_files <- c(
    file.path(paths$manifests, "phase-component-model-registry.csv"),
    file.path(paths$manifests, "woody-pct-model-registry.csv")
  )
  if (!all(file.exists(registry_files))) {
    stop(
      "F01 model registers are missing. Run quarto render task-f01.qmd -P refit:true."
    )
  }

  registry <- bind_rows(lapply(
    registry_files,
    read_csv,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )) |>
    mutate(
      comparison_group = paste(response, analysis, sep = " | ")
    ) |>
    mutate(
      aic_rank = if_else(
        fit_status == "fit",
        rank(aic, ties.method = "min"),
        NA_real_
      ),
      delta_aic = if_else(
        fit_status == "fit",
        aic - min(aic[fit_status == "fit"], na.rm = TRUE),
        NA_real_
      ),
      .by = comparison_group
    ) |>
    arrange(comparison_group, aic_rank, model_id)
  write_csv(registry, file.path(paths$manifests, "model-comparison.csv"))
}

publication_table(read.csv("outputs/fuel/manifests/model-comparison.csv"))







Provisional model-review register
We’ll pull the AIC leaders into a shorter review register so unresolved convergence or residual problems are easy to find. Its status column identifies what needs follow-up before scientific acceptance and gives RD04 a record to consult when drafting the fuel display.


Code
# tbl-fuel-provisional-models
# tbl-fuel-provisional-models
if (recompute) {
  selection_log <- registry |>
    filter(fit_status == "fit", aic_rank == 1) |>
    mutate(
      diagnostic_follow_up = rowSums(
        across(starts_with("dharma_"), ~ !is.na(.x) & .x < 0.05)
      ) >
        0
    ) |>
    transmute(
      response,
      analysis,
      provisional_aic_leader = model_id,
      aic,
      pd_hessian,
      dharma_uniformity_p,
      dharma_dispersion_p,
      dharma_outlier_p,
      dharma_zero_inflation_p,
      selection_status = case_when(
        !pd_hessian ~ "rejected pending convergence resolution",
        diagnostic_follow_up ~ "requires diagnostic follow-up",
        TRUE ~ "eligible for scientific review"
      ),
      selection_rationale = "This is the AIC-leading predeclared candidate, not a final selection. Retain only after diagnostic and scientific review."
    )

  write_csv(
    selection_log,
    file.path(paths$manifests, "model-selection-log.csv")
  )
}

Table 2: Provisional AIC-leading fuel models generated by F01; these are not final selections.










We’ve separated the fuel components, checked the pre- and post-PCT pairing, and fitted and compared candidate models for the phase-specific loads and woody vegetation change. Most matched transects had less standing woody vegetation after PCT, giving us an indicator of its potential contribution to surface fuels; we still cannot translate that reduction directly into a measured slash load. The component definitions also keep litter and duff estimates confined to the pre-PCT phase, where their separation is defensible. Both the direct-difference and joint-phase approaches now have saved fits and diagnostics, with AIC leaders that remain provisional pending scientific review. These results give RD04 a basis for estimating and displaying fuel loads and the woody phase contrast, while retaining the alternative fits for sensitivity review and keeping the interpretation clear for the publication’s fuel Results.

title: RD02 - regeneration basal area display
text:
Question and goals
How does regeneration basal area differ among retained-overstory treatments ten years after harvest, and how much does that answer depend on how we represent species and sampling groups? We’ll review the thesis results, make the current statistical choices explicit, and examine existing sensitivity evidence before presenting the publication estimates.
The products are a redwood/tanoak (RW/TO) Results figure and a four-category supplement table, including Douglas-fir and other species. Basal area is measured in m² ha⁻¹; this task does not analyze stem counts. Following the model comparison, we retain the four separate species models as the final selection. The RW/TO Results figure and four-category supplement table are accepted for downstream publication drafting. The occurrence sensitivity supports the decision to include treatment in redwood’s zero component; the other three categories retain constant zero probabilities. RD02 is complete with those updated models and displays.

title: RD02 - regeneration basal area display
text:
Setup and execution
The F01 bundle supplies shared readers and display functions; RD02-specific analysis stays here. An ordinary render reviews saved evidence. -P recompute:true refreshes calculations from saved models; -P refit:true also refits them. -P refit_diagonal:true fits only the two diagonal candidates and recomputes the comparisons from the other saved fits. Missing models are prerequisites, not permission to refit. -P refit_zero:true fits only the six new zero-process alternatives and refreshes their sensitivity results; it reads the constant-zero comparison models without refitting them. -P recompute_zero:true refreshes this sensitivity and the selected publication outputs from saved fits. A full recomputation also refreshes the earlier constant-zero covariance comparisons.
We’ll use one set of data, paths, and labels. The 256 rows represent four categories on 64 vegetation plots, nested in 16 treatment macro plots at four sites. Recomputing overwrites current outputs directly, so a failed run requires completing the affected sequence before treating its outputs as current.

title: RD02 - regeneration basal area display
text:
Thesis results
The thesis selected ba_ha ~ treat * spp + (1 | site:spp), with a log-link Gamma positive component and species-specific zero and dispersion components. Its Results wrapper predicted with type = "response" and re.form = NA: zeros are included, but random effects are set to zero. That is different from integrating over their distributions, despite the prediction documentation’s use of the term population-level.
The figure redraws the actual thesis means and response-scale asymptotic 95% intervals, recovered from the saved thesis regen_all emmeans objects under R 4.3.2. The exporter verifies all 16 cells against the saved-model zero-effect reference and verifies estimate ± qnorm(.975) × SE. We show RW/TO without the thesis significance arrows. Negative lower limits are retained: they reflect the original normal approximation, not a claim that basal area can be negative. The publication estimates use an integrated target and positive intervals.
We’ll copy the committed historical evidence without loading thesis models in the publication environment, then draw its focal-species figure.

# fig-rd02-historical-reference

Observed sampling context
