Figure 3: Observed zero proportions (crosses) and fitted probabilities with approximate 95% intervals for constant and site-varying zero submodels. Site-model predictions condition on fitted zero-process site effects. Each site has 16 vegetation plots per species category. These are exploratory fits; four sites provide limited information about their variance.





The site-varying fits shrink the observed differences toward a common probability. Redwood and tanoak shrink almost completely; Douglas-fir retains the clearest fitted site gradient. Other-species occurrence differs between Camp 6 and the remaining sites, but the fit gain does not offset the AIC penalty.
We’ll now propagate the zero-model changes into the publication estimand: expected basal area including zeros, integrated over independent site and macro-plot effects. The logistic-normal expectation and its derivatives enter the full covariance calculation above. The zero and positive processes are independent in these specifications; a site-only occurrence multiplier is constant across treatments, so it preserves their mean ratios. Treatment zero effects can change those ratios. We check the baseline against its constant-zero means and SEs and check alternative ratios against the separate positive-Gamma and occurrence contributions. Intervals remain asymptotic; refitted bootstrap coverage and formal boundary-variance tests are not assessed here.


Code
# rd02-zero-estimates
if (zero_recompute) {
  zero_estimates <- bind_rows(lapply(names(zero_models), function(id) {
    sp <- zero_fit$spp[match(id, zero_fit$model_id)]
    integrated_means(zero_models[[id]], id, species = sp)
  })) |> left_join(select(zero_fit, model_id, zero_structure), by = "model_id")
  accepted <- read.csv(file.path(selected_root, "tables/rd02-constant-zero-species-estimates.csv"))
  baseline <- filter(zero_estimates, zero_structure == "constant")
  index <- match(paste(baseline$spp, baseline$treat), paste(accepted$spp, accepted$treat))
  stopifnot(!anyNA(index), max(abs(baseline$estimate/accepted$estimate[index] - 1)) < 1e-7,
            max(abs(baseline$se/accepted$se[index] - 1)) < 1e-7)
  zero_estimates <- zero_estimates |>
    left_join(transmute(baseline, spp, treat, baseline_mean = estimate, baseline_width = ucl-lcl),
              by = c("spp", "treat")) |>
    mutate(mean_change_percent = 100*(estimate/baseline_mean - 1),
           interval_width_change_percent = 100*((ucl-lcl)/baseline_width - 1)) |>
    group_by(model_id) |> mutate(ratio_to_GS = estimate/estimate[treat == "gs"]) |> ungroup()
  ratio_check <- zero_estimates |> group_by(spp, treat) |>
    summarise(spread = diff(range(ratio_to_GS[zero_structure %in% c("constant", "site")])), .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(nrow(zero_estimates) == 40L, max(abs(ratio_check$spread)) < 1e-3)

Figure 4: Expected regeneration basal area including modeled zeros under alternative zero submodels. All candidates retain the same positive-Gamma specification. Points integrate independent conditional and zero-process random effects; ranges are full-covariance log-scale delta-method 95% intervals for means. Treatment-dependent zeros are selected for redwood; other categories retain constant zeros. Species panels use different vertical scales.





Allowing site variation alone leaves redwood and tanoak estimates essentially unchanged. Douglas-fir means increase by about 0.64%, with interval widths about 8–10% larger; other-species means increase by about 0.09%, with widths about 2% larger. Site-only occurrence variation therefore has little effect on the current population-average basal-area conclusions, despite visible fitted site differences for Douglas-fir.
Redwood treatment-dependent occurrence has a larger practical effect: expected GS basal area rises from 12.66 to 15.51 m² ha⁻¹, while HD falls from 0.93 to 0.68. The estimated GS-to-HD ratio increases from about 13.6 to 22.7, while the GS > LD > HA > HD ordering remains. Treatment-plus-site estimates are almost identical. These changes reflect occurrence, not a changed positive-Gamma response, and their weak AIC advantage remains a qualification of the selected model.
This sensitivity separates site and treatment variation in occurrence and shows where the initial constant-zero assumption matters for interpretation. The publication displays below now use treatment-dependent redwood zeros and retain constant zeros for tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species. Four sites, sparse tanoak zeros, independent component random effects, boundary variances, and unassessed bootstrap interval behavior limit inference.

title: RD02 - regeneration basal area display
text:
Selected species models and inference
We retain four separate hurdle-Gamma models, all with treatment in the positive component and site and nested macro-plot random intercepts. Redwood now also has treatment in its zero component; the other three categories retain constant zero probabilities. Dispersion remains constant within each category. The redwood choice represents treatment differences in occurrence as well as growth where regeneration is present. We retain its small AIC advantage as a qualification and do not describe it as decisive evidence.
For redwood, the zero component has no random effects. Its mean including zeros is
\[
M_t=(1-p_t)\exp\left\{x_t^{\mathsf T}\beta+
\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{site}}+\sigma^2_{\mathrm{macro}}}{2}\right\}.
\]
We average over the modeled distributions of site and macro-plot intercepts, rather than condition on fitted site effects. The lognormal integration factor is about 1.298 for redwood and is common across its treatments; treatment-specific nonzero probabilities determine the occurrence contribution. Gamma dispersion does not require a residual correction to this mean.
We propagate uncertainty through the full parameter covariance matrix, including positive- and zero-component treatment coefficients, both log random-effect SDs, and their estimated covariances. If \(h_t=\log M_t\) and \(g_t\) is its gradient, \(\operatorname{Var}(h_t)\approx g_t^{\mathsf T}Vg_t\). We exponentiate \(h_t\pm1.96\operatorname{SE}(h_t)\) for positive 95% confidence intervals. These describe uncertainty in population means, not new-plot variability. The integration and delta calculations above retain the prediction, numerical-gradient, and quadrature checks. Four-site estimation, boundary macro-plot variances, and unassessed bootstrap coverage limit this approximation.
Treatment comparisons here remain descriptive estimates and ratios. We have not performed formal pairwise contrasts; confidence-interval overlap is not a test. A formal ratio contrast would use \(\log M_t-\log M_u\) and its joint gradient with the same covariance matrix, rather than treat the two means as independent. Intervals are conditional on the selected specification and omit model-selection uncertainty.
We’ll refresh the canonical estimates, numerical register, and residual plots from the exact saved fits already evaluated above. This selects an existing fitted candidate without changing its fitting inputs or refitting. All three other species retain their constant-zero models.


Code
# rd02-selected-refresh
if (zero_recompute) {
  selected_fit_rows <- selected_var_rows <- selected_diag_rows <- selected_opt_rows <- list()
  selected_estimate_rows <- list()
  for (sp in species_order) {
    id <- if (sp == "rw") "rw_zi_treatment" else paste0(sp, "_site_macro")
    m <- read_saved_model(file.path(selected_root, "models", paste0(id, ".rds")), "RD02")
    check <- read_saved_model(file.path(selected_root, "models", paste0(id, "-bfgs.rds")), "RD02")
    record <- zero_fit[zero_fit$model_id == id, ]
    stopifnot(nrow(record) == 1L, m$fit$convergence == 0, m$sdr$pdHess,
      check$fit$convergence == 0, abs(check$fit$objective-m$fit$objective) < 1e-4,
      identical(names(fixef(m)$zi), if (sp == "rw") names(fixef(m)$cond) else "(Intercept)"),
      length(VarCorr(m)$zi) == 0L)
    selected_fit_rows[[sp]] <- record |>
      mutate(species = unname(species_labels[sp])) |>
      select(spp, species, model_id, zero_formula, n, n_zero, k, log_likelihood, AIC,
             convergence, pd_hessian, max_abs_gradient, warnings)
    selected_var_rows[[sp]] <- rd02_variances(m, id) |>
      mutate(spp = sp) |> select(spp, group, n_groups, variance, sd)
    sim <- publication_simulate_residuals(m, n = simulations, seed = seed, refit = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
    selected_diag_rows[[sp]] <- rd02_tests(sim, id, "species_plot_rows") |>
      mutate(spp = sp) |> select(spp, test, statistic, p_value)
    selected_opt_rows[[sp]] <- data.frame(spp = sp, convergence = check$fit$convergence,
      pd_hessian = check$sdr$pdHess,
      objective_difference_from_nlminb = check$fit$objective-m$fit$objective,
      warnings = record$bfgs_warnings)
    selected_estimate_rows[[sp]] <- integrated_means(m, id, sp)
    png(file.path(selected_root, "diagnostics", paste0(sp, "-dharma.png")), width=1800, height=1000, res=160)
    plot(sim)
    dev.off()
    png(file.path(selected_root, "diagnostics", paste0(sp, "-by-treatment.png")), width=1200, height=1000, res=160)
    plotResiduals(sim, form = model.frame(m)$treat)
    dev.off()
  }
  selected_estimates <- bind_rows(selected_estimate_rows) |>
    mutate(spp = factor(spp, levels = species_order),
      treat = factor(treat, levels = c("gs", "ld", "ha", "hd")),
      species = unname(species_labels[as.character(spp)]), unit = "m2 ha-1",
      estimand = "species-specific arithmetic expected basal area including zeros, integrated over site and macro-plot random effects",
      interval_method = "95% log-scale delta method using full parameter covariance") |> arrange(spp, treat)
  index <- match(paste(selected_estimates$model_id, selected_estimates$treat),
                 paste(zero_estimates$model_id, zero_estimates$treat))
  stopifnot(nrow(selected_estimates) == 16L, !anyNA(index),
    !anyDuplicated(selected_estimates[c("spp", "treat")]),
    max(abs(selected_estimates$estimate/zero_estimates$estimate[index]-1)) < 1e-7,
    max(abs(selected_estimates$se/zero_estimates$se[index]-1)) < 1e-7)
  tables <- list("fit-register" = bind_rows(selected_fit_rows), "variances" = bind_rows(selected_var_rows),
    "diagnostics" = bind_rows(selected_diag_rows), "optimizer-checks" = bind_rows(selected_opt_rows),
    "estimates" = selected_estimates)
  for (name in names(tables)) write.csv(tables[[name]],
    file.path(selected_root, "tables", paste0("rd02-selected-species-", name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
}

title: RD02 - regeneration basal area display
text:
Summary and model decision
We confirm four separate hurdle-Gamma models as the final selection, with treatment effects and site and nested macro-plot intercepts in the positive component. Redwood also includes treatment in its zero component; tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species retain constant zero probabilities. No selected zero component has random effects. This represents species-specific growth and occurrence responses. The constant-zero covariance comparison shows why a joint diagonal parameterization adds no explanatory power to its corresponding separate fits. Common-variance site-by-species alternatives lead that earlier comparison; the selected redwood zero model improves its own baseline AIC by only 0.85. We retain this modest fit evidence as a qualification of the scientifically motivated selection. Treatment ordering is stable within species, but absolute means, interval widths, and some cross-species ordering depend on model structure. The historical figure now represents the actual thesis target; the publication figure represents integrated expected basal area including zeros.
RD02 is complete. The four selected models, updated RW/TO Results figure, and four-category supplementary table are accepted for downstream publication drafting. The zero-process sensitivity remains the evidence for the redwood occurrence decision and the alternatives we did not select. Reported treatment comparisons remain descriptive; formal pairwise contrasts have not been performed. Boundary variances, four-site estimation, constant zero probabilities outside redwood, and unassessed bootstrap interval behavior remain material limitations, as does the four-category diagonal fit’s BFGS Hessian warning at the same objective. Cross-species covariance and model-selection uncertainty are not estimated. Completion does not add new pairwise significance claims.
RT01 owns regeneration Results drafting; M02 will adapt this framework for Methods. Sprout-height analysis stays in RD03 and broader cohort interpretation in D01. Those tasks should use the canonical estimates and link here for the model decision and its qualifications.

title: RT03 - fuel Results narrative
text:
Purpose, inputs, and scope
With the fuel estimates assembled, we’ll work out which patterns the Results should report and how to describe their uncertainty. This page draws on the F01 component/model record and RD04 inference and display record. The F01 and RD04 task pages own their execution order and handoff. The shared sections/results.qmd assembles the Results; RT03 maintains the shared fuel subsection in sections/fuel-results.qmd.
Results subsection in the working manuscript reports phase-specific fuel reference means followed by the matched woody standing-vegetation contrast. Its working allocation is 1.5–2 manuscript pages, approximately 500 words excluding the figure, table, captions, and review note; final pagination depends on journal formatting.

title: RT03 - fuel Results narrative
text:
Implemented source and review decisions







Source or finding
Implementation in RT03




Thesis analysis/thesis/results.qmd, fuel subsections
Retain the pre-PCT, post-PCT, and vegetation-transition sequence, using current publication values throughout.


Revised component definitions
Report woody and herbaceous vegetation separately; distinguish modeled litter and duff before PCT; omit post-PCT forest-floor estimates.


RD04 inference review
Use equally site-weighted, random-effect-integrated arithmetic mean loads including zeros, rather than the thesis zero-random-effect references.


Joint woody phase model
Report its four pre-minus-post mean reductions and covariance-aware confidence intervals, consistent with the woody load panel. Do not use the separate Student-t difference-model estimates.


Thesis significance and causal wording
Replace inherited p-values with descriptive treatment rankings. Report exclusion of zero only for the four computed woody-change intervals; dead-fuel phase comparisons have no paired-change tests here.


Slash and design interpretation
Describe potential surface-fuel contribution, not measured slash deposition; avoid attributing the entire phase transition to PCT.


Numerical provenance
Draw inline narrative values and the shared companion table from rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv; do not carry forward the unsourced coarse-wood grand mean noted in the audit.



Review products: the fuel Results draft and existing nine-panel figure and caption. The companion values table is accepted for the publication supplement; its source is sections/rd04-fuel-estimates-table.qmd.
Acceptance tests: each quantitative claim is traceable to the current figure/CSV; point-estimate rankings are not presented as pairwise tests; intervals describe uncertainty in means, not new-transect variation; the standing-woody contrast is not a direct slash measure or an isolated causal PCT effect. Scientific model acceptance and narrative review remain open. Acceptance of the supplementary table does not mark RT03 accepted or complete.

title: RT03 - fuel Results narrative
text:
Draft Results and numerical source
The hidden setup loads the shared F01 helpers and enables automatic chunk labels before any code is displayed.
The Results values need to stay aligned with the figure as the analysis develops. We’ll read the saved RD04 means and intervals and format them for inline use, without recalculating inference. The saved formatter carries those estimates with it and is refreshed on each render. The draft below puts the values in context, moving from phase-specific fuel conditions to matched woody change.


Code
# rt03-fuel-narrative-values
fuel_results <- read.csv(
  "outputs/fuel/tables/rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
fuel_components <- c(
  one = "1-hour fuel",
  ten = "10-hour fuel",
  hundred = "100-hour fuel",
  coarse = "1,000-hour fuel",
  woody = "Woody vegetation",
  herb = "Herbaceous vegetation",
  litter = "Litter (pre-PCT only)",
  duff = "Duff (pre-PCT only)",
  reduction = "Woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)"
)
fuel_phases <- c(
  pre = "Pre-PCT",
  post = "Post-PCT",
  change = "Vegetation difference"
)
fuel_value <- function(
  component,
  phase,
  treatment,
  interval = FALSE,
  digits = 1L
) {
  cell <- fuel_results[
    fuel_results$component == fuel_components[[component]] &
      fuel_results$phase == fuel_phases[[phase]] &
      fuel_results$treatment == treatment,
  ]
  stopifnot(nrow(cell) == 1L)
  value <- formatC(cell$estimate, format = "f", digits = digits)
  if (interval) {
    value <- paste0(
      value,
      " (95% CI ",
      formatC(cell$lcl, format = "f", digits = digits),
      " to ",
      formatC(cell$ucl, format = "f", digits = digits),
      ")"
    )
  }
  value
}

# Save the function with the data it uses so other pages can render inline values.
environment(fuel_value) <- list2env(list(fuel_results = fuel_results,
  fuel_components = fuel_components, fuel_phases = fuel_phases), parent = baseenv())
dir.create("outputs/helpers", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(fuel_value, "outputs/helpers/fuel-value.rds")

title: RT03 - fuel Results narrative
section: Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning
text:
Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning

Dead fuel loading
Fuel measurements ten years after harvest characterized conditions before and after precommercial thinning (PCT) across the four retention treatments (Figure 1). Following PCT, group selection (GS) and low-density dispersed retention (LD) showed the largest estimated increases in fine dead-fuel loads and reductions in woody standing vegetation. These treatments also had the highest post-PCT fine dead-fuel loads. Pre-PCT dead-fuel estimates suggested subtler, component-specific treatment patterns. Fuel loads are reported as model-estimated means, with 95% confidence intervals. Woody and herbaceous standing vegetation are reported separately, as are pre-PCT litter and duff. All loads and load differences below are in Mg ha-1.
Before PCT, estimated 1-hour fuel loads were highest in high-density aggregated retention (HA; 1.2) and lowest in GS (0.6), with LD and high-density dispersed (HD) retention intermediate. Estimated 10-hour loads ranged from 2.8 in HD to 3.8 in GS, and 100-hour loads from 9.0 to 11.5 in those same treatments. The 1,000-hour class had larger mean loads, ranging from 30.2 in LD to 49.6 (95% CI 25.9 to 95.0) in GS. Uncertainty was substantial for this coarse-wood component across treatments.
The separated forest-floor components showed different treatment patterns. Pre-PCT litter estimates ranged from 12.6 in LD to 18.4 in GS; HA and HD were intermediate. Duff estimates were lowest in HA, at 19.3 (95% CI 14.5 to 25.8), and highest in HD, at 35.5 (95% CI 26.6 to 47.4), with GS and LD both near 28–29. These are model-derived forest-floor loads based on the estimated litter-depth boundary. Post-PCT litter and duff were not estimated because the forest-floor boundary could not be distinguished reliably in the presence of slash and suspended foliage.
After PCT, estimated 1-hour loads were about 2.4–2.7 in GS, LD, and HD, and 1.4 in HA. The 10-hour estimates were ordered GS (9.6), LD (5.9), HA (4.1), and HD (3.3). The 100-hour estimates followed the same order, from 19.6 (95% CI 11.8 to 32.8) in GS to 7.5 (95% CI 4.6 to 12.2) in HD. Post-PCT 1,000-hour means ranged from 25.2 in HA to 53.9 in GS, with wide confidence intervals. These rankings describe estimated loads; they do not establish pairwise treatment differences. The separate dead-fuel phase estimates are reference conditions, without paired phase-change tests in this display.


Standing vegetation and woody vegetation difference
Pre-PCT woody standing-vegetation means were greatest in GS (39.9), followed by LD (26.5), HD (18.8), and HA (14.7). Post-PCT means were 2.0–2.9 across treatments. The joint phase model estimated pre-minus-post reductions of 37.4 (95% CI 13.4 to 61.4) in GS, 24.5 (95% CI 9.0 to 40.0) in LD, 11.8 (95% CI 3.6 to 20.0) in HA, and 16.6 (95% CI 5.5 to 27.6) in HD. All four reduction intervals excluded zero. Their uncertainty includes the pre/post covariance; the ordering of reduction estimates alone does not test differences among treatments.
Herbaceous standing-vegetation means were small relative to woody loads: 0.24–0.59 before PCT and 0.11–0.35 afterward, with broad relative uncertainty. The woody reduction represents an inferred potential contribution to surface fuels. It does not measure slash deposition or reconcile standing-vegetation loss with changes in downed fuel classes. Without a contemporaneous unthinned comparison, the phase transition does not isolate a causal PCT effect.


Fuel inventory






Figure 1: Fuel components by retention treatment before and after precommercial thinning (PCT). Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.

title: Development workflow
text: The task register records current status and inputs. Each task page explains its purpose, calculations, findings, and decisions. Develop the manuscript from figures and tables → results → methods → discussion → introduction → abstract → title.

title: Development workflow
text:
Review sequence
Direction for review → Approved to execute → In progress → Pending review → Accepted (or Revision requested) → Complete.
Queued work remains queued until authorized. A completed analytical record does not imply scientific acceptance. Keep decisions with the task that made them; consumers explain how they use those decisions.

title: Development workflow
text:
Render and recompute
From the publication directory, quarto render builds the entire site using saved results. Add -P recompute:true to refresh calculations from saved models, or -P refit:true to fit models explicitly. Both parameters default to false.
For faster iteration, only re-render pages affected by requested changes.
Calculations overwrite their current files directly. A failed calculation can leave partially updated outputs. Preserve separate copies explicitly when comparing results. There are no staging directories or promotion steps.
Read each task as purpose and rationale → code → result → interpretation. Each block explains why it is needed before it runs. Results appear directly after their generating code, even when also saved for downstream tasks. Review renders display the saved result in that same place; if (recompute) guards the calculation inside the cell, leaving its table or figure visible in both modes.

text:

The planned 1–1.5-page subsection should explain how the reported quantities are estimated, with expanded comparisons and secondary species detail linked in the supplement. That keeps the route from field observations to reported estimates easy to follow.
For sprout heights, the RD03 review and proposal now identify the selected-clump sampling target, four-site treatment replication, shared year-5 measurement in adjacent increments, and the distinction between zero-effect and integrated predictions. title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Study area and design
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Analysis
Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses will be retained as supplementary material.

Regeneration basal area
Basal area was modeled separately for redwood, tanoak, Douglas-fir, and other species using zero-inflated Gamma mixed models with a conditional log link. Treatment was a fixed effect; site and macro plot nested within site were random intercepts. Each species category had its own intercept-only zero and dispersion components. Each model used 64 vegetation-plot observations from four sites and 16 macro plots. Arithmetic mean basal area included modeled zeros and integrated over both fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. Confidence intervals for the means were calculated using the log-scale delta method with the full parameter covariance, including random-effect variance uncertainty. Redwood and tanoak estimates are displayed in the Results; estimates for all four categories are reported in the supplement.


Fuel loads and PCT contrast
Reported values are model-based arithmetic mean loads, including modeled zeros and integrating over fitted random effects, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts.
These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
section: Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning
text:
Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning

Dead fuel loading
Fuel measurements ten years after harvest characterized conditions before and after precommercial thinning (PCT) across the four retention treatments (Figure 2). Following PCT, group selection (GS) and low-density dispersed retention (LD) showed the largest estimated increases in fine dead-fuel loads and reductions in woody standing vegetation. These treatments also had the highest post-PCT fine dead-fuel loads. Pre-PCT dead-fuel estimates suggested subtler, component-specific treatment patterns. Fuel loads are reported as model-estimated means, with 95% confidence intervals. Woody and herbaceous standing vegetation are reported separately, as are pre-PCT litter and duff. All loads and load differences below are in Mg ha-1.
Before PCT, estimated 1-hour fuel loads were highest in high-density aggregated retention (HA; 1.2) and lowest in GS (0.6), with LD and high-density dispersed (HD) retention intermediate. Estimated 10-hour loads ranged from 2.8 in HD to 3.8 in GS, and 100-hour loads from 9.0 to 11.5 in those same treatments. The 1,000-hour class had larger mean loads, ranging from 30.2 in LD to 49.6 (95% CI 25.9 to 95.0) in GS. Uncertainty was substantial for this coarse-wood component across treatments.
The separated forest-floor components showed different treatment patterns. Pre-PCT litter estimates ranged from 12.6 in LD to 18.4 in GS; HA and HD were intermediate. Duff estimates were lowest in HA, at 19.3 (95% CI 14.5 to 25.8), and highest in HD, at 35.5 (95% CI 26.6 to 47.4), with GS and LD both near 28–29. These are model-derived forest-floor loads based on the estimated litter-depth boundary. Post-PCT litter and duff were not estimated because the forest-floor boundary could not be distinguished reliably in the presence of slash and suspended foliage.
After PCT, estimated 1-hour loads were about 2.4–2.7 in GS, LD, and HD, and 1.4 in HA. The 10-hour estimates were ordered GS (9.6), LD (5.9), HA (4.1), and HD (3.3). The 100-hour estimates followed the same order, from 19.6 (95% CI 11.8 to 32.8) in GS to 7.5 (95% CI 4.6 to 12.2) in HD. Post-PCT 1,000-hour means ranged from 25.2 in HA to 53.9 in GS, with wide confidence intervals. These rankings describe estimated loads; they do not establish pairwise treatment differences. The separate dead-fuel phase estimates are reference conditions, without paired phase-change tests in this display.


Standing vegetation and woody vegetation difference
Pre-PCT woody standing-vegetation means were greatest in GS (39.9), followed by LD (26.5), HD (18.8), and HA (14.7). Post-PCT means were 2.0–2.9 across treatments. The joint phase model estimated pre-minus-post reductions of 37.4 (95% CI 13.4 to 61.4) in GS, 24.5 (95% CI 9.0 to 40.0) in LD, 11.8 (95% CI 3.6 to 20.0) in HA, and 16.6 (95% CI 5.5 to 27.6) in HD. All four reduction intervals excluded zero. Their uncertainty includes the pre/post covariance; the ordering of reduction estimates alone does not test differences among treatments.
Herbaceous standing-vegetation means were small relative to woody loads: 0.24–0.59 before PCT and 0.11–0.35 afterward, with broad relative uncertainty. The woody reduction represents an inferred potential contribution to surface fuels. It does not measure slash deposition or reconcile standing-vegetation loss with changes in downed fuel classes. Without a contemporaneous unthinned comparison, the phase transition does not isolate a causal PCT effect.


Fuel inventory






Figure 2: Fuel components by retention treatment before and after precommercial thinning (PCT). Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction
Developing and maintaining multiaged stand structures requires silvicultural systems that create and sustain cohorts of different ages within the same stand (O’Hara, 1998; Schütz, 2002). Retention systems can retain a range of tree densities in dispersed or aggregated patterns and can be used to maintain multiaged stands or transform formerly even-aged stands (Mitchell & Beese, 2002).
Coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) is well suited to this objective because it regenerates reliably by stump sprouting and can grow beneath a retained overstory. Its response to light is nevertheless important: reduced access to light can limit sprout vigor and persistence (Berrill et al., 2018; Muma et al., 2022; O’Hara et al., 2007). Tanoak (Notholithocarpus densiflorus) is also shade tolerant and a vigorous resprouter, making its response relevant to both stand development and management of competing vegetation (Berrill et al., 2021; O’Hara et al., 2017).
Silvicultural decisions that promote regeneration also influence the fuel conditions in which later management and fire occur. This paper therefore examines regeneration under varying overstory retention and describes surface fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning as reference information for integrated silvicultural, fuels, fire, and potential modeling applications.
We use 10-year measurements from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment to evaluate regeneration responses among retention treatments and to report fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including their PCT-associated contrast. Redwood and tanoak provide the primary regeneration focus, with other species retained as descriptive context where useful. Fuel components will be presented in a publication-specific form after their analytical specification is reviewed.

Mitchell, S. J., & Beese, W. J. (2002). The retention system: reconciling variable retention with the principles of silvicultural systems. The Forestry Chronicle, 78(3), 397–403. https://doi.org/10.5558/tfc78397-3


Muma, R., Webb, L. A., Zald, H. S. J., Boston, K., Dagley, C. M., & Berrill, J.-P. (2022). Dynamics of stump sprout regeneration after transformation to multiaged management in coast redwood forests. Forest Ecology and Management, 515, 120236. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foreco.2022.120236


O’Hara, K. L. (1998). Silviculture for structural diversity: a new look at multiaged systems. Journal of Forestry, 96(7), 4–10. https://doi.org/10.1093/jof/96.7.4a

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
section: What height adds to the regeneration story
text:
What height adds to the regeneration story
Does retained overstory leave redwood with a developing cohort of tall sprouts, even where regeneration basal area is strongly reduced? Height helps distinguish the size attained by leading sprouts from the amount of regeneration occupying an area. We’ll review the thesis evidence before choosing a publication model and the smallest useful set of displays. The publication’s regeneration-first direction makes redwood development the main question, with tanoak providing ecological context; this task does not repeat RD02’s basal-area result.
Phase Two implements the reference and design/covariance comparison. The human review and Phase Three handoff distinguishes exploratory fits from accepted publication results. All 692 recorded clumps are the intended cohort, as confirmed in human review on 6 November 2026. Final model selection, calibrated uncertainty, and publication displays remain pending.

Evidence reviewed and numerical limits
The review uses the thesis Methods, Results, and Discussion, their QMD sources, analysis/analysis/sprouts_import_data.qmd, and analysis/analysis/sprout_modeling.qmd. On 6 November 2026 we also inspected analysis/sprout_modeling.rda and analysis/wrangled_sprouts.rda read-only in thesis R 4.3.2 with its existing library (glmmTMB 1.1.11). We checked saved calls, model frames, coefficients, variance components, convergence flags, and zero-random-effect predictions. Neither the thesis environment nor its saved objects was changed. Its startup reported an out-of-sync project, locale warnings, and a glmmTMB build under R 4.3.3; this inspection is not an environment validation.
The saved analysis contains 692 clumps: 334 redwood and 358 tanoak, across four sites and 16 treatment-unit macro plots. There are 2,076 height observations and 1,384 increments, with no missing outcomes in these saved frames. Treatment cell sizes range from 72 to 91 clumps for redwood and 78 to 95 for tanoak. The imported increments exactly equal \((H_5-H_1)/4\) and \((H_{10}-H_5)/5\). Those checks establish the content of the saved analysis, not the completeness of the original field cohort or the reason clump counts differ.
At the initial review, committed publication exports covered fuels and regeneration basal area, not sprout heights. An intentional sprout export in the thesis environment, with identifiers, factor levels, missingness, selection information where available, and historical prediction references, is a prerequisite for publication fitting. We must also reconcile those exports with the original workbook and field history before assuming that the complete saved frames imply no attrition. The existing exporter and manifest should be extended when we implement the analysis. Phase One below implements that boundary and documents what field history remains unavailable.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
section: What the thesis models actually assume
text:
What the thesis models actually assume
The measured response is the height of the tallest sprout within a selected clump at each visit. The leading stem can change between visits. Consequently, the increment is change in clump maximum height, annualized over an interval, rather than necessarily the elongation of one continuously tracked stem. The saved variable named tree identifies the repeated clump record for this purpose. It is not evidence that the same individual sprout remained tallest.
Clumps were selected to be well distributed within macro plots. Redwood sampling also balanced clumps with and without residual standing trees. That is not a documented equal-probability sample of all clumps or stems. An unweighted model describes this selected clump cohort; generalizing to an area-wide clump mean requires a defensible sampling assumption or known inclusion weights. It cannot be interpreted as mean height of all regeneration, mean height of retained PCT trees, survival, recruitment, or an area-based productivity measure.

Interval height increment
The saved minc_sel is the source’s minc15, with Gaussian response and identity link. Writing period for the factor stored as year (5 = years 1–5; 10 = years 5–10), its conditional mean formula is:
ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + (1 | clump) + (0 + spp | macro).
The source uses globally unique tree and plot IDs for clump and macro. Residual dispersion is ~ spp * period * treat, allowing 16 species–treatment– period residual scales. The macro effect is a two-species unstructured covariance matrix: separate species variances and one correlation, not a separate common macro intercept plus an additional species effect. The clump intercept variance is common to both species. There is no separate site term in this saved model. The glmmTMB covariance documentation explains the distinction between unstructured and diagonal species effects.
This specification allows species-specific treatment differences and species-specific changes between periods. It constrains the period change to be identical across all treatments within a species: neither treatment × period nor the three-way mean interaction is present. A lack of those terms does not establish equal temporal responses. Conditional residuals are independent after the clump and macro effects; the clump intercept induces nonnegative covariance between its two increments. Random effects are Gaussian, independent across grouping levels, and independent of predictors. Residual heterogeneity does not replace either clustering or a suitable within-clump covariance.
The saved fit reports convergence code 0 and a positive-definite Hessian. Clump SD is 0.115 m yr-1; macro SDs are 0.141 for redwood and 0.059 for tanoak, with correlation 0.254. These estimates support inspecting unequal species variation, without establishing that this covariance structure is adequate or precisely estimated from 16 macro plots.


Height at year 10
The saved ht10_sel is mht1011, a Gaussian response with a log link:
ht ~ treat * spp + (0 + spp | macro) + (1 | site); residual dispersion is ~ spp * treat (eight residual scales).
The response itself is not log-transformed. Residual variation is additive on the metre scale, while the conditional mean is positive and multiplicative in the predictors. A Gaussian distribution can still generate negative heights: a log link restricts its mean, not its support. The model assumes a shared site intercept on the log-mean scale and correlated species-specific macro intercepts. No clump intercept is needed for one response per clump.
This fit also reports convergence code 0 and a positive-definite Hessian. Macro SDs on the log-mean scale are 0.195 for redwood and 0.159 for tanoak, with correlation 0.475. Site SD is approximately 0.000021, effectively at the boundary. This is weak information about a site variance, not proof that blocking is scientifically irrelevant. Four sites remain four treatment replicates per treatment; the hundreds of clumps are subsamples.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
section: Validity and precision of the thesis interpretation
text:
Validity and precision of the thesis interpretation

Patterns supported by the saved means
The following historical values were reproduced from the saved coefficients and response predictions with random effects set to zero. They are not new publication estimates. Increment means give the two intervals equal weight.

Increment units are m yr-1; height units are m. The extra digits make this audit identifiable, not biologically precise. The year-10 means match the rendered thesis’s 10.38–5.81 m and 5.13–3.12 m ranges, rather than the older 10.29–6.16 m and 5.12–3.04 m values left in the modeling notebook.
The broad descriptive pattern is coherent: leading redwood sprouts were taller and had larger increments than tanoak; GS means were largest; HA and HD were lower, particularly for redwood. These observations add a size dimension to RD02’s area-based regeneration response. They do not establish every adjacent treatment difference or a continuous response to measured light.


Corrections needed before publication

The model and prose disagree about interactions. The thesis year-10 Results say the model lacks species × treatment and therefore gives parallel treatment comparisons. The saved fit contains that interaction, as do the Methods’ final specification. The increment notebook also says an interaction is absent after assigning a model that contains it. Distinguish an AIC-preferred reduced candidate from the retained research-question model. With a log link, omitting the interaction would impose common treatment ratios, not common metre differences. Nonsignificant interaction tests do not establish equivalence.
The species response claim needs its own contrast. In the retained increment model, treatment coefficients alone refer to the reference species, tanoak. Redwood treatment differences combine those coefficients with the interaction. A range of coefficient p values is not an omnibus treatment test. The saved redwood-versus-tanoak difference in the HD–GS increment response is about -0.227 m yr-1, with an individual asymptotic Wald p value of 0.029. This does not supply a multiplicity-adjusted family test, but it shows why the blanket statement that the interaction was nonsignificant is imprecise. Publication claims need explicitly defined contrasts and uncertainty.
Period means mix historical versions and weighting conventions. The text’s 0.80 to 0.67 m yr-1 for redwood and 0.39 to 0.34 for tanoak agrees approximately with equally weighted treatment predictions (0.803 to 0.670; 0.385 to 0.344). The thesis temporal prediction call uses newdata = NULL, averaging observed rows; that gives 0.804 to 0.672 and 0.384 to 0.342 in the saved fit. We should use one declared weighting rule and regenerate prose from its results. The period decreases are 0.132 and 0.041 m yr-1 in every treatment by model construction, not eight independently demonstrated changes.
Equal-period averaging is not the nine-year annual rate. The two intervals last four and five years. An equal-period mean is \((I_1+I_2)/2\); the annualized years 1–10 change is \((4I_1+5I_2)/9\). Neither includes years 0–1. Label these quantities explicitly; prefer separate intervals if temporal development is the scientific point.
Response-scale prediction is not random-effect integration. The thesis helper explicitly uses re.form = NA, setting random effects to zero, as described in the prediction documentation. For identity-link increments, zero-mean random-effect integration leaves the mean unchanged. For log-link year-10 height it gives \(M_{st}=\exp\{x_{st}^{\mathsf T}\beta+(\tau^2_{\mathrm{site}}+
\tau^2_{\mathrm{macro},s})/2\}\) under this model. This is integration over log-mean random effects; there is no lognormal residual correction for a Gaussian response with a log link. The current factors are about 1.019 for redwood and 1.013 for tanoak. The distinction is small here but must remain explicit, especially if we change the hierarchy or family. As in RD02, treatment-constant integration factors preserve within-species ratios.
Asymptotic intervals have limited replication behind them. The thesis prediction-to-emmeans helper uses df = Inf and reconstructs mean covariance from mean and pairwise-difference SEs. The resulting comparison arrows are not ordinary confidence bars or an independent validation of contrasts. Reproduce their covariance, contrast scale, and adjustment before retaining any historical pairwise claim. The printed p = 0 is rounding, never an exact zero probability. New displays should show intervals for means and report selected contrasts separately. Model selection, sampling selection, measurement error, and covariance-structure uncertainty are not included in those Wald intervals. Convergence flags alone do not verify residual fit or interval coverage.



What the biological interpretation can support
Tallest-clump height is relevant to the potential size of a future retained sprout. It does not identify the stems actually retained after PCT or demonstrate their subsequent performance. Height and basal area may respond differently because one describes selected clump maxima and the other integrates stem sizes and occurrence per area. That difference is informative rather than contradictory.
Treatments combine overstory amount and spatial arrangement. HA versus HD is the direct arrangement comparison at similar target retention; a small, uncertain difference does not establish that aggregation has no effect. The treatment gradient is consistent with light limitation, but height models alone do not isolate light from other treatment-associated conditions or establish a species’ physiological shade tolerance. An SDI or light model would ask a different question.
The thesis suggestion that roughly 32–38 m2 ha-1 is an upper retention bound for sustaining redwood growth beyond ten years exceeds what four categorical treatments and a ten-year record establish. We can say that leading redwood sprouts continued gaining height under the studied high-retention treatments, at lower estimated rates than GS. We cannot estimate a continuous threshold, long-term sustainability, stand yield, or an optimal cutting cycle from these fits.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
text:
Proposed revisions and sensitivity tests
Our working target is arithmetic mean tallest-clump height, or its interval change, for the sampled clump cohort under each treatment. We should standardize comparisons across equally weighted treatments and sites and state whether means average the four observed sites or integrate an exchangeable site population. The latter matches RD02’s presentation, but adds a generalization assumption that four sites estimate poorly. Neither target automatically represents all clumps per hectare. If field information supports redwood sampling-stratum weights, report that explicitly rather than silently redefining the population.
We’ll keep year-10 height as the primary size endpoint and interval increment as the complementary temporal endpoint. Start with the thesis response families as reference fits, retain species-specific treatment means, and test the following limited alternatives. These are proposed candidates, not an invitation to choose whichever produces the strongest treatment significance.








Proposed change or test
Assumption retained, relaxed, or introduced
Evidence needed for a decision




Represent site blocking in both endpoints; compare site fixed effects with site random intercepts, retaining macro clustering
Replaces the increment model’s independence of different treatment units at the same site. Fixed sites condition inference on these four blocks; random sites assume exchangeability and a Gaussian site distribution.
Treatment estimates and intervals under both specifications, variance boundaries, and four leave-one-site-out fits. Do not delete design clustering solely for AIC or a near-zero estimate.


Compare the joint unstructured species macro effects with diagonal effects and separate species fits, allowing species-specific clump variance for increments
Diagonal effects remove cross-species macro covariance; separate fits also remove shared variance constraints. The thesis shares clump variance across species. Separate species-specific site variances relax the common site variance but are weakly identified from four sites.
Same response rows and family for the covariance comparison; inspect variance estimates, correlations, optimizer agreement, and treatment uncertainty. Separate fits can describe species means but do not supply covariance for a species-difference test.


Retain treatment × species; compare increment means with treat * spp * period
Relaxes the imposed common period change across treatments. The full mean model permits treatment-specific slowing or acceleration within each species.
Period-change contrasts and their species/treatment differences, with intervals. Absence of a detected interaction is not temporal equivalence. A reduced model needs a scientific interpretation as well as fit support.


Compare saturated dispersion with spp * period and additive treatment dispersion for increments; spp + treat versus spp * treat for year 10
Reduced dispersion pools residual scales across some cells. It does not pool treatment means or solve clustering. Separate-species fits permit their own residual scales.
Residual spread and tails by species, treatment, period, and macro plot; fit stability and changes in interval widths. Retain supported heterogeneity rather than simplifying to improve significance.


Test within-clump covariance of the two increments; compare the shared intercept with a directly estimated two-period covariance
The thesis allows only nonnegative residual association through a common clump intercept. An unstructured two-period covariance permits either sign and different variances, but needs an identifiable parameterization.
Estimate covariance after macro/site effects. Do not add a full two-period covariance on top of freely varying period residual variances and a clump intercept: these components cannot all be identified from two outcomes per clump.


Compare year-10 Gaussian identity/log links and positive Gamma(log); use a lognormal alternative only if residual evidence warrants it
Identity link models additive metre effects; log links model proportional conditional effects. Gamma imposes positive support and variance proportional to squared mean within a dispersion group. Lognormal assumes Gaussian log-height residuals and needs residual as well as random-effect integration for arithmetic means.
Observed/predicted distributions and lower-tail/negative-height simulation frequency, residual scale, convergence, and estimates on the same arithmetic-mean target. Do not use Gamma for increments if valid zero or negative increments exist in the audited input.


Fit heights at years 1, 5, and 10 jointly as a targeted sensitivity, with categorical age and identifiable within-clump covariance
Avoids treating two differences sharing year 5 as conditionally independent. Categorical age avoids assuming linear growth or extrapolating a curve from three visits. It introduces a model for the three-level covariance and all-age means.
Derive \((M_5-M_1)/4\), \((M_{10}-M_5)/5\), and year-10 means from one fit, retaining covariance. Compare these estimands with the two-endpoint analysis; use the joint model as primary only if its assumptions and stability are preferable.


Compare zero-effect, integrated, and observed-site standardized predictions; equal-period and duration-weighted summaries
Changes the prediction target or averaging weights, not necessarily the fitted model. Integration assumes the specified random-effect distribution represents the target population.
Reconcile implementation by direct prediction, analytic integration where available, and numerical checks. Propagate variance-parameter uncertainty for integrated means. Never label a change of estimand as a biological change.




Why the shared year-5 measurement matters
If measured heights have independent errors \(e_1,e_5,e_{10}\), then the two increment errors are \((e_5-e_1)/4\) and \((e_{10}-e_5)/5\). Their covariance is \(-\operatorname{Var}(e_5)/20\). A persistent clump growth tendency can instead produce positive association. The thesis clump intercept represents the latter but cannot by itself represent the former. This derivation does not prove that the fitted covariance is wrong; it identifies a scientifically motivated sensitivity with a possible consequence for uncertainty in growth-rate change. With no replicate height measurements, measurement-error variance cannot be separately learned without additional assumptions or external precision data. Two intervals also cannot establish a general serial-correlation process.


Selection and uncertainty sequence
First audit identity, measurement definitions, interval lengths, original missing records, and any mortality or leader replacement notes. Resolve the redwood residual-tree sampling stratum: its indicator is described in the import source but omitted from the selected columns. If recoverable, use it for a targeted sampling/composition sensitivity, recognizing that residual-tree status is treatment-related and adjusting for it changes the question. Likewise, conditioning on year-1 height estimates later development at a common post-treatment size; it is not a correction for a pretreatment covariate and should not replace the unadjusted treatment comparison. Do not treat absent/dead clumps as zero heights without field justification, or invent missing-data weights from these complete saved frames.
Next fit the reference and design/covariance alternatives on identical audited rows. Use maximum likelihood when comparing fixed-effect structures. Compare AIC within the same endpoint and likelihood basis; AIC across height and increment responses is meaningless. A model for log(height) needs the response-transformation Jacobian before comparing its likelihood with original-height models. Keep scientific mean terms needed for planned contrasts even when their individual coefficients are weak. Avoid stepwise selection over every interaction.
Require numerical convergence, a usable Hessian, and agreement under a second optimizer for plausible finalists. Inspect boundary variances, residual and simulation diagnostics by species/treatment/period, within-clump association, macro-level residual patterns, and influential sites. Four leave-one-site-out analyses diagnose sensitivity; they do not turn three-site fits into precise estimates or justify dropping an inconvenient site. A small AIC difference or nonsignificant diagnostic is weak evidence, as RD02 demonstrated.
Compare finalist mean estimates and intervals for GS versus HD (retention contrast), HA versus HD (arrangement contrast), and the second-minus-first interval change. Add species differences in those responses only with a joint covariance model or a paired resampling method that preserves sites, macro plots, and both species. Predeclare contrast families and a multiplicity approach (for example Holm adjustment for a small confirmatory family); keep other contrasts exploratory. GS–HD compares complete treatments, not an isolated continuous basal-area effect. Use metre differences for size and m yr-1 differences for increment; report ratios as an additional interpretation only when useful. Avoid claiming equal responses without a biologically justified equivalence margin.
For the preferred specification, assess the sensitivity of Wald uncertainty with a refitted parametric bootstrap that preserves the hierarchy, heterogeneity, and repeated measurements, including variance-parameter uncertainty in integrated means. Predeclare a seed and simulation count, report failed/boundary refits, and examine stability of interval endpoints. This assesses inference under the fitted model, not robustness to unmodeled sampling bias. Resampling just four sites nonparametrically is a weak sole basis for coverage. A within-site treatment randomization sensitivity is possible only after confirming the assignment scheme in the experimental record; it tests a different, design-based null. Intervals conditional on a selected model still omit model-selection uncertainty.
RD02 motivates design-aware clustering, explicit estimands, species-specific variance checks, optimizer checks, and caution with four-site asymptotics. Its hurdle-Gamma occurrence process does not transfer automatically: these height records are selected clumps, not vegetation plots with recorded absence. We should select the simplest scientifically adequate height model and report material sensitivity, even if the treatment ordering remains unchanged.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
text:
Proposed publication displays

1. Main figure: attained height and temporal change
Use one four-panel figure, with redwood and tanoak as columns. The top row shows year-10 mean tallest-clump height by treatment (GS, LD, HA, HD), in metres, with 95% intervals. The bottom row shows the estimated change in annualized increment, years 5–10 minus years 1–5, by treatment, with 95% intervals and a zero reference line. Use a common height scale across species for direct size comparison and a common increment-change scale across species in the bottom row. Keep the species colors/shapes used in RD02 and state that the sampling units differ.
This joins attained size with the genuinely additional temporal question without repeating the treatment-averaged increment figure. It can show a continued redwood height advantage alongside slower later development. Do not imply treatment-specific temporal evidence if the selected mean model constrains all treatment changes to be equal: in that case collapse the bottom row to one species-wise change panel, labeled as averaged across treatments. If temporal evidence proves too fragile or secondary, retain the year-10 row as the main figure and move the temporal display to the supplement.
Provisional caption structure: “Tallest-sprout development in sampled redwood and tanoak clumps under four retained-overstory treatments. Upper panels show modeled mean height at year 10; lower panels show later-minus-earlier annualized height change. Points and ranges denote arithmetic means or contrasts and their 95% confidence intervals [state site standardization/integration and uncertainty method after selection]. Heights follow the tallest stem in each clump at each visit, which need not be the same stem. Clumps are subsamples of 16 treatment units in four sites; intervals describe mean uncertainty.” Define treatment abbreviations in the final caption. Do not include significance arrows or infer pairwise differences from overlapping mean intervals.


2. Optional companion: interval rates without averaging them away
If absolute growth rates matter for the management interpretation, use two species panels with treatment on the x-axis and paired points for years 1–5 and 5–10, in m yr-1, with uncertainty. A light connector within each treatment can show the interval change; it is not a continuous annual growth trajectory. Use the same vertical scale for both species. Prefer equally weighted site summaries as subdued observed context, with four site symbols per treatment, over a dense cloud that makes hundreds of clumps look like treatment replicates. Label observed summaries separately from model estimates and omit them if they obscure the intervals.
This is an alternative temporal view or a supplement, not a second mandatory main-text figure duplicating the lower row above. It preserves the thesis’s approximate 0.80-to-0.67 redwood and 0.39-to-0.34 tanoak story while allowing the revised analysis to reveal treatment dependence. Keep full estimates, interval definitions, planned contrasts, and sensitivity evidence in a companion table. No invented confidence limits or schematic results are needed at this stage.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
text:
Where this leaves RD03
The thesis provides credible preliminary evidence that selected leading redwood sprouts attained greater height under lighter retention and continued developing under the higher-retention treatments. Its model/prose mismatch, selected-clump sampling target, imposed temporal structure, and limited treatment replication prevent us from carrying its precision and significance language forward unchanged. The proposed tests separate changes to biological response assumptions from changes to covariance and prediction targets. A compact size-plus-time display can then complement RD02 without implying that tall sprouts alone establish successful cohort recruitment or a long-term retention threshold. Model choice, interval calibration, and final captions remain open until these tests are run.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
section: Phase One: audited inputs and human review
text:
Phase One: audited inputs and human review
Can we trace every modeled clump to the workbook, and what population can those records describe? This first phase implements the audit and export prerequisites in the selection sequence. Phase Two will fit the reference and limited design/covariance candidates; later selection, bootstrap uncertainty, and display acceptance follow that comparison. The phases make the existing sequence explicit without accepting any candidate model in advance.
We exported both workbook sheets, the saved wide measurements with original and renumbered identifiers, the historical response frames, and plain prediction references in thesis R 4.3.2. The exporter checks every imported column against the workbook and reproduces the saved long frames. It preserves the historical factor levels (LIDE, SESE; GS, LD, HA, HD), row order, and missing values. No fitted model crosses the publication boundary. The manifest protects the workbook, saved objects, import/model sources, Methods, and existing thesis environment. The thesis startup still reports its existing synchronization, locale, and package-build warnings; no packages or lockfiles were changed. Replaying the shared exporter also rewrote the existing fuel/regeneration RDS files with a UTF-8 serialization header. Read-back comparisons with the committed baseline confirmed identical R objects, and the historical CSV checksums are unchanged; those analyses therefore require no numerical refresh.
The following audit runs in publication R 4.6.2 using only exported measurements. An ordinary render reads saved audit tables; -P recompute:true refreshes these deterministic calculations. -P refit:true also runs the Phase Two fits below; it does not refit any thesis analysis or RD02 model.


Show audit setup and helpers
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(tidyr) })
recompute <- isTRUE(params$recompute) || isTRUE(params$refit) || isTRUE(params$refit_temporal)
input <- "inputs/thesis/sprouts"
out <- "outputs/sprouts/phase-one"
read_audit <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(out, paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
write_audit <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, file.path(out, paste0(name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
if (recompute) {
  dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  d <- readRDS(file.path(input, "measurements.rds"))
  raw <- readRDS(file.path(input, "workbook-all.rds"))
  tallest <- readRDS(file.path(input, "workbook-tallest.rds"))
  frames <- readRDS(file.path(input, "historical-frames.rds"))
}



Identity, repeated measurements, and interval definitions
We require unique original clump keys and a one-to-one map to the saved clump IDs. Each macro plot must belong to one site and treatment, each site must have all four treatments, and every clump must have three heights and two increments. The numerical checks below use a tolerance of 10-12 m yr-1 for spreadsheet roundoff; no height or increment is replaced or rounded in the input.


Code
if (recompute) {
  keys <- raw[c("Site", "Plot", "Species", "Tree")]
  macros <- distinct(d, plot, site, treat, original_plot)
  err5 <- max(abs(d$ht_inc5 - (d$ht5 - d$ht1) / 4))
  err10 <- max(abs(d$ht_inc10 - (d$ht10 - d$ht5) / 5))
  height_index <- match(paste(frames$dht$tree, frames$dht$year),
    paste(rep(d$tree, each = 3), rep(c(1, 5, 10), nrow(d))))
  inc_index <- match(paste(frames$dinc$tree, frames$dinc$year),
    paste(rep(d$tree, each = 2), rep(c(5, 10), nrow(d))))
  checks <- data.frame(check = c("Unique original site/plot/species/clump keys",
    "Unique saved clump IDs and source rows", "16 macros, one treatment per site",
    "Three historical heights per clump", "Two historical increments per clump",
    "Year-10 frame matches wide heights", "Years 1-5 increment = (H5-H1)/4",
    "Years 5-10 increment = (H10-H5)/5"),
    passed = c(!anyDuplicated(keys), !anyDuplicated(d$tree) && !anyDuplicated(d$source_row),
      nrow(macros) == 16L && !anyDuplicated(macros$plot) &&
        all(table(macros$site, macros$treat) == 1),
      nrow(frames$dht) == 3L * nrow(d) && !anyNA(height_index) &&
        !anyDuplicated(frames$dht[c("tree", "year")]) &&
        all(frames$dht$ht == c(t(as.matrix(d[c("ht1", "ht5", "ht10")])))[height_index]),
      nrow(frames$dinc) == 2L * nrow(d) && !anyNA(inc_index) &&
        !anyDuplicated(frames$dinc[c("tree", "year")]) &&
        all(frames$dinc$ht_inc == c(t(as.matrix(d[c("ht_inc5", "ht_inc10")])))[inc_index]),
      nrow(frames$dht10) == nrow(d) && !anyDuplicated(frames$dht10$tree) &&
        all(frames$dht10$ht == d$ht10[match(frames$dht10$tree, d$tree)]),
      err5 < 1e-12, err10 < 1e-12))
  stopifnot(all(checks$passed))
  write_audit(checks, "identity-checks")
}

All available workbook rows are accounted for in the saved analysis. The Age10all sheet supplies 692 clumps, while Age10tallest50tpha contains a 320-row subset with the same original keys and heights. The latter has ten clumps per site/treatment/species cell and ranks 1–10; it is an outcome-selected subset, not additional replication or an attrition record. We retain the full 692-row cohort for the planned comparison and do not apply the workbook’s saved display filter. The original plot numbers and clump labels remain available alongside the saved globally unique plot and tree factors.
We count clumps within the actual treatment units because these counts reveal sampling composition without treating clumps as independent treatment replicates. The selected-height subset is counted separately to expose the selection.


Code
if (recompute) {
  counts <- d |> group_by(site, treat, spp) |>
    summarise(n_clumps = n(), n_missing_height = sum(is.na(ht1) | is.na(ht5) | is.na(ht10)),
      n_tallest_subset = sum(in_tallest_sheet), .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(nrow(counts) == 32L, sum(counts$n_clumps) == 692L,
    all(counts$n_tallest_subset == 10L), sum(d$in_tallest_sheet) == nrow(tallest),
    all(tallest$HT10rank <= 10), all(d$in_tallest_sheet == (d$ht_rnk10 <= 10)))
