Human review and Phase Two handoff
The available records now support a reproducible analysis of the selected, recorded clump cohort, retaining all 692 rows. They do not resolve whether the workbook was assembled only from surviving or otherwise eligible clumps. We found no original enrollment roster, mortality/absence ledger, per-visit leader IDs, or inclusion probabilities in the workbook, import/model sources, Methods, work log, or relevant repository notes; the workbook has no cell comments or additional sheets documenting those events. The tally of roughly 25 clumps per species per macro plot is insufficient to reconstruct an attrition denominator. These are missing field-history evidence, not failed numerical checks.
Human review on 6 November 2026 confirmed the recorded cohort as the intended target and defined the indicator as a residual redwood tree left on the clump following harvest. GS has no such trees because all trees were cut. Unequal counts may reflect too few available clumps in some blocks; no original roster was supplied to verify that explanation. No sampling weights, zero-height replacements, survival claims, or unobserved leader histories have been inferred. If new field information changes inclusion or measurements, refresh the export and this audit before fitting.
The next agent should read this section and the candidate plan, verify export integrity with python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --inputs-only --protected, and use inputs/thesis/sprouts/measurements.rds in the publication environment. Preserve the exported factor coding and original ID crosswalk; use all rows, not the tallest-ten subset. The historical frames and 24 prediction cells provide reproduction references, not publication estimates. Start Phase Two with the thesis reference fits and the limited site-blocking, species-macro covariance, and increment temporal-mean alternatives on identical rows. Use ML for fixed-effect comparisons, retain design clustering, and record convergence, Hessian, variance boundaries, second-optimizer agreement, and leave-one-site-out sensitivity. Do not add an unidentified full two-period covariance on top of unrestricted residual variances and a clump intercept.
Before reporting publication means, resolve observed-site versus exchangeable-site standardization and predeclare contrast families and multiplicity handling. Keep residual-tree adjustment as an explicitly conditional sensitivity, subject to the GS overlap limitation. Bootstrap calibration and final displays follow model review; RT02, M02, and D02 remain queued. Human review should precede the next phase.
Phase One establishes traceable inputs and exposes a consequential selection limitation that complete analytical frames alone concealed. It also recovers a sampling indicator that can inform a carefully bounded sensitivity. The main scientific limitation remains generalization beyond the selected recorded clumps; model fitting cannot recover the missing field history or establish survival.

title: RD03 - sprout-height display
section: Phase Two: design, covariance, and explanatory candidates
text:
Phase Two: design, covariance, and explanatory candidates
How much of the apparent treatment and temporal pattern survives a model that respects the four-site experiment, and does a residual redwood on the same clump help explain sprout development? We retain every audited clump and compare a limited set of scientifically motivated alternatives. Fits here are exploratory publication candidates, not accepted Results. Human review has authorized this cohort and clarified residual-tree status; it has not supplied sampling weights or a survival history.
Our working target is arithmetic mean tallest-clump height or interval change in this selected cohort, standardized equally over the four observed sites. For log-link models we integrate the Gaussian macro effect for point estimates; fixed sites avoid generalizing a site distribution from four blocks. Random-site candidates instead describe an exchangeable-site population and are explicitly labeled as a different target. The provisional intervals below propagate fixed mean-coefficient uncertainty only, holding random-effect variance estimates fixed. They are a comparison aid, not final coverage claims. Phase Three must include variance-parameter uncertainty and assess finite-replication calibration.
Before fitting, we reserve four redwood contrasts for a possible confirmatory family: GS minus HD and HA minus HD in year-10 height, and the same two treatment differences in later-minus-earlier annual increment. Phase Three will apply Holm adjustment across those four tests if retained. Cell-wise temporal changes, tanoak context, covariance comparisons, and residual-tree associations remain exploratory. No significance-based model search or equivalence claim is intended.

Fitting and prediction helpers
The helpers keep ML fitting, convergence evidence, and arithmetic-mean prediction consistent across candidates. A saved model is required for recomputation; only refit:true authorizes the complete fitting sequence. The focused refit_temporal:true mode fits the added species-specific temporal-macro candidates, their optimizer checks, and site omissions while reading every other saved fit. We retain warnings and unsuccessful numerical fits in the register rather than quietly discarding them. Model RDS files remain ignored; tables and diagnostic figures remain versioned.


Show fitting and prediction helpers
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(glmmTMB); library(ggplot2); library(DHARMa) })
p2 <- "outputs/sprouts/phase-two"
p2_read <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(p2, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
p2_write <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, file.path(p2, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
if (recompute) {
  for (folder in c("models", "tables", "figures"))
    dir.create(file.path(p2, folder), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  wide <- readRDS(file.path(input, "measurements.rds"))
  inc <- bind_rows(mutate(wide, period = "5", ht_inc = ht_inc5),
                   mutate(wide, period = "10", ht_inc = ht_inc10)) |>
    mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("5", "10")))
  stopifnot(nrow(wide) == 692L, nrow(inc) == 1384L, !anyNA(wide$ht10), !anyNA(inc$ht_inc))
  fits <- list(); fit_records <- list(); fit_data <- list()
}
rd_fit <- function(id, mean, dispersion, data, endpoint, stage = "candidate",
                   family = gaussian(if (endpoint == "height") "log" else "identity"),
                   second_optimizer = FALSE) {
  path <- file.path(p2, "models", paste0(id, ".rds"))
  if (isTRUE(params$refit) || (isTRUE(params$refit_temporal) && grepl("^i_(LIDE|SESE)_macro", id))) {
    message("RD03 fitting ", id)
    warnings <- character()
    control <- if (second_optimizer)
      glmmTMBControl(optimizer = optim, optArgs = list(method = "BFGS"),
                     optCtrl = list(maxit = 10000, reltol = 1e-10), rank_check = "stop") else
      glmmTMBControl(optCtrl = list(iter.max = 3000, eval.max = 5000), rank_check = "stop")
    m <- withCallingHandlers(glmmTMB(mean, dispformula = dispersion, data = data,
      family = family, REML = FALSE, na.action = na.fail, control = control),
      warning = function(w) { warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
    attr(m, "rd03_warnings") <- paste(unique(warnings), collapse = "; ")
    saveRDS(m, path)
  } else {
    if (!file.exists(path)) stop("Missing saved RD03 fit: ", id, ". Explicit refit:true is required.")
    m <- readRDS(path)
  }
  stopifnot(nobs(m) == nrow(data), identical(rownames(model.frame(m)), rownames(data)))
  if ("tree" %in% names(model.frame(m)))
    stopifnot(identical(as.character(model.frame(m)$tree), as.character(data$tree)))
  ll <- logLik(m)
  fit_records[[id]] <<- data.frame(model_id = id, stage = stage, endpoint = endpoint,
    fit_status = "fit", n = nobs(m), n_clumps = n_distinct(data$tree), n_sites = n_distinct(data$site),
    mean = paste(deparse(formula(m)), collapse = " "),
    dispersion = paste(deparse(formula(m, component = "disp")), collapse = " "),
    family = family(m)$family, link = family(m)$link, parameters = attr(ll, "df"),
    log_likelihood = as.numeric(ll), AIC = AIC(m), convergence = m$fit$convergence,
    pd_hessian = isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess), max_gradient = max(abs(m$sdr$gradient.fixed)),
    warnings = attr(m, "rd03_warnings"))
  fits[[id]] <<- m
  fit_data[[id]] <<- data
  m
}
rd_usable <- function(m) m$fit$convergence == 0 && isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess)
rd_variance <- function(m, id) {
  bind_rows(lapply(names(VarCorr(m)$cond), function(group) {
    v <- VarCorr(m)$cond[[group]]
    ix <- which(lower.tri(v, diag = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)
    data.frame(model_id = id, group = group, term1 = rownames(v)[ix[, 1]],
      term2 = colnames(v)[ix[, 2]], covariance = v[ix],
      correlation = attr(v, "correlation")[ix],
      boundary_sd_below_1e_4 = sqrt(diag(v))[ix[, 1]] < 1e-4 | sqrt(diag(v))[ix[, 2]] < 1e-4)
  }))
}
rd_means <- function(m, data, endpoint, id) {
  stopifnot(rd_usable(m))
  grid <- expand.grid(site = levels(droplevels(data$site)), treat = levels(droplevels(data$treat)),
    spp = levels(droplevels(data$spp)),
    period = if (endpoint == "increment") levels(data$period) else "year10",
    KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for (v in c("site", "treat", "spp")) grid[[v]] <- factor(grid[[v]], levels = levels(data[[v]]))
  if (endpoint == "increment") grid$period <- factor(grid$period, levels = levels(data$period))
  grid$plot <- data$plot[1]; grid$tree <- data$tree[1]
  ff <- delete.response(terms(lme4::nobars(formula(m))))
  X <- model.matrix(ff, grid)
  beta <- fixef(m)$cond
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(X), names(beta)))
  eta <- drop(X %*% beta)
  stopifnot(max(abs(predict(m, newdata = grid, type = "link", re.form = NA) - eta)) < 1e-8)
  multiplier <- rep(1, nrow(grid))
  vc <- VarCorr(m)$cond
  random_site <- "site" %in% names(vc)
  if (family(m)$link == "log") {
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
      v <- sum(vapply(names(vc), function(group) {
        z <- vc[[group]]
        if (nrow(z) == 1L) z[1, 1] else z[paste0("spp", grid$spp[i]), paste0("spp", grid$spp[i])]
      }, numeric(1)))
      multiplier[i] <- exp(v / 2)
    }
  }
  mu <- family(m)$linkinv(eta) * multiplier
  J <- X * as.numeric(family(m)$mu.eta(eta) * multiplier)
  cells <- unique(grid[c("spp", "treat", "period")])
  W <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), function(j) {
    z <- grid$spp == cells$spp[j] & grid$treat == cells$treat[j] & grid$period == cells$period[j]
    as.numeric(z) / sum(z)
  }, numeric(nrow(grid))))
  G <- W %*% J
  covariance <- G %*% as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond) %*% t(G)
  ans <- data.frame(model_id = id, cells, estimate = drop(W %*% mu),
    se = sqrt(diag(covariance)), target = if (random_site) "exchangeable sites; random effects integrated" else
      "four observed sites equally weighted; macro effects integrated",
    uncertainty = "provisional Wald; random variances held fixed")
  ans$lcl <- ans$estimate - qnorm(.975) * ans$se
  ans$ucl <- ans$estimate + qnorm(.975) * ans$se
  list(table = ans, covariance = covariance, gradient = G,
       coefficient_covariance = as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond))
}
rd_contrasts <- function(z, endpoint) {
  a <- z$table; rows <- list()
  add <- function(w, label, spp) {
    est <- sum(w * a$estimate)
    # Form the contrast gradient first: subtracting nearly equal cell
    # covariances loses precision for changes constrained to be identical.
    g <- drop(t(w) %*% z$gradient)
    se <- sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% z$coefficient_covariance %*% g))
    rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <<- data.frame(model_id = a$model_id[1], spp = spp,
      contrast = label, estimate = est, se = se, lcl = est - qnorm(.975) * se,
      ucl = est + qnorm(.975) * se, uncertainty = a$uncertainty[1])
  }
  for (sp in unique(as.character(a$spp))) {
    if (endpoint == "height") {
      for (tr in c("GS", "HA")) add(as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr) -
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == "HD"), paste0(tr, " minus HD height"), sp)
    } else {
      changes <- lapply(levels(wide$treat), function(tr)
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr & a$period == "10") -
        as.numeric(a$spp == sp & a$treat == tr & a$period == "5"))
      names(changes) <- levels(wide$treat)
      for (tr in names(changes)) add(changes[[tr]], paste0(tr, " later minus earlier"), sp)
      for (tr in c("GS", "HA")) add(changes[[tr]] - changes$HD,
        paste0(tr, " minus HD period change"), sp)
    }
  }
  bind_rows(rows)
}




Reference and blocked joint models
We first reproduce the two thesis specifications from the exported measurements. The increment reference omits site blocking and constrains temporal change within each species; the alternatives add site, diagonal species-macro effects, and then the full treatment × species × period mean. All joint candidates use the same rows within an endpoint and ML. The two height families and reduced dispersion candidates are bounded sensitivities, not a replacement for residual review. AIC comparisons are meaningful only within the same endpoint and response rows; fixed versus random sites also change the generalization assumption.
Use the model-comparison table to see which changes improve fit without adding unnecessary parameters. Compare AIC only within height or within increment; check convergence and pd_hessian before interpreting a model’s estimates.

The new reference fits reproduce all 24 historical prediction cells: the largest differences are 0.00000374 m for year-10 height and less than 0.000000002 m yr-1 for increments. Adding fixed sites changes the height comparison little; allowing cross-species macro covariance improves AIC by only 0.47 relative to diagonal effects. Random-site variances approach zero in both endpoints, but that does not remove the experimental blocks from the design.
Among the blocked diagonal height candidates, Gaussian(log) has the lowest AIC; identity and Gamma(log) are higher by 5.64 and 24.86. Pooling treatment dispersion raises AIC by 11.10. The full increment mean raises AIC by 6.42 relative to the otherwise matched reduced mean: treatment-specific temporal responses are not strongly supported by this likelihood comparison. We nevertheless retain the full mean as an exploratory sensitivity so that its uncertainty is visible; the reduced mean imposes parallel responses rather than demonstrating them.


Species-specific and two-period covariance sensitivities
Separate species models relax the shared site and clump-variance assumptions. For increments, we compare the saturated treatment/period dispersion with a period-only version, then replace its clump intercept and residual variances with one unstructured two-period clump covariance. The latter includes no additional clump intercept or free residual variance. It can represent negative association but pools covariance across treatments within a species; thus it does not also reproduce treatment-specific dispersion. The period-only intercept fit makes that restriction visible rather than confounding both changes. This follows the identifiable formulation in the glmmTMB covariance documentation.
One more covariance question matters for temporal inference: a single macro intercept cancels from a within-clump period difference. We therefore also fit species-specific two-period macro effects, retaining the clump intercept and treatment/period dispersion. These allow treatment units to differ in their temporal responses. The temporal-macro fits keep the full mean structure and remain identifiable because each macro contains many repeated clumps.
The next table compares these alternatives within each species. In particular, compare i_SESE_macro with i_SESE, and i_LIDE_macro with i_LIDE, to assess whether allowing macro plots to change between periods improves fit.

The separate-species increment fits estimate clump variances of 0.0461 for redwood and 0.0080 for tanoak, indicating that a shared variance is a substantial restriction. The period-only clump covariances are positive (correlations 0.615 and 0.405), and their unstructured fits have essentially the same likelihood as the corresponding intercept fits. Negative association is permitted but is not estimated here. This does not separately identify measurement-error variance.
Allowing macro effects to differ by period lowers AIC by 11.72 for redwood and 14.21 for tanoak relative to their separate-species saturated-dispersion intercept fits. Macro correlations are high (0.920 and 0.876), but unequal period variances leave nonzero treatment-unit variation in temporal change. This is a more consequential covariance improvement than permitting a negative clump covariance, and it should carry forward to Phase Three. All full-cohort candidates converge with positive-definite Hessians; stability under reduced site replication is a separate question below.


A residual tree on the clump
We explore whether a retained redwood on a clump explains development within LD, HA, and HD, adjusting for treatment and observed site. GS is structurally code 0 and tanoak has no defined indicator; neither supplies a residual-tree comparison. The height candidate estimates one common log-mean association across the three treatments; the increment candidate allows that association to differ by period while retaining treatment-specific temporal means. Baseline and adjusted likelihoods use identical redwood rows. These are post-treatment associations that can reflect clump selection or local conditions, not causal direct/indirect effects of retaining a tree. We do not condition the primary treatment comparison on this indicator or invent area-wide stratum weights.
The fit table asks whether adding residual-tree status explains enough variation to justify the extra model terms. Compare rh_residual with rh_base, and ri_residual with ri_base; each pair uses exactly the same clumps.

      increment_5_10 = mean(ht_inc10), .groups = "drop"), "residual-tree-observed")
  assoc <- list()
  for (id in c("rh_residual", "ri_residual")) {
    m <- fits[[id]]; beta <- fixef(m)$cond; V <- as.matrix(vcov(m)$cond)
    for (period in if (id == "rh_residual") "year10" else c("5", "10")) {
      w <- setNames(rep(0, length(beta)), names(beta)); w["residual_rw"] <- 1
      if (period == "10") w[grep("residual_rw:period10|period10:residual_rw", names(beta))] <- 1
      est <- sum(w * beta); se <- sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% V %*% w))
      logged <- id == "rh_residual"
      f <- if (logged) exp else identity
      assoc[[length(assoc) + 1L]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, period = period,
        effect = if (logged) "residual-present / absent height ratio" else "residual-present minus absent m yr-1",
        estimate = f(est), lcl = f(est - qnorm(.975) * se), ucl = f(est + qnorm(.975) * se),
        uncertainty = "exploratory Wald; selected retained-treatment clumps")
    }
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(assoc), "residual-tree-associations")
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records)[vapply(fit_records, function(x) x$stage == "residual_tree", logical(1)), ], "residual-tree-comparison")
}

The height ratio is 1.050 (exploratory 95% Wald interval 0.950–1.160); increment associations are +0.031 and +0.016 m yr-1, with intervals spanning both suppression and augmentation. Comparable means and planned contrasts
The arithmetic predictions below expose sensitivity to mean and covariance assumptions. We average sites equally, integrate log-link random effects analytically, and check the fixed design against direct zero-effect prediction. Reference random-site models have a different population target, labeled in the saved table. Separate-species fits cannot provide cross-species contrasts. Intervals are unadjusted, provisional Wald summaries with variance components held fixed. AIC, interval overlap, or a small temporal coefficient alone does not establish an accepted model or equivalent temporal responses.
The mean table gives the scale of the modeled responses under each treatment: height in metres for h_diagonal, and annual height change in m/year for i_full. It provides context for the direct comparisons that follow.

The blocked diagonal height candidate estimates redwood means of 10.57, 8.04, 6.92, and 5.93 m for GS, LD, HA, and HD. The GS–HD difference is 4.64 m; the HA–HD difference is 0.99 m with substantially greater uncertainty relative to its size. The separate redwood height fit gives nearly identical differences (4.65 and 0.96 m). These are candidate estimates, not accepted publication claims.
The redwood temporal-macro fit estimates later-minus-earlier changes of -0.159, -0.163, -0.064, and -0.120 m yr-1. Its GS–HD and HA–HD differences in change are -0.039 and +0.056 m yr-1; both provisional intervals span zero. In particular, tanoak’s four temporal-change intervals all span zero once temporal macro variation is represented, despite all four point estimates being negative. Neither the thesis’s parallel-response interpretation nor a claim of equal slowing across treatments follows from these results.


Numerical agreement and influential sites
We check plausible blocked candidates and the residual-tree associations with BFGS started independently of the primary nlminb fit. We record likelihood and prediction differences without converting agreement into evidence of scientific adequacy. Four leave-one-site-out fits each of the blocked height, joint full increment, and two separate temporal-macro candidates retain treatment-unit clustering and average the remaining three sites equally. They diagnose sensitivity to particular blocks; they do not justify excluding a site or estimate model-selection uncertainty.
The optimizer table checks whether two fitting algorithms reach essentially the same answer. Small objective and prediction differences support numerical reliability; they do not establish that the model describes the biology well.


Code
if (recompute) {
  optimizer_ids <- c("h_diagonal", "h_identity", "h_gamma", "i_full", "i_disp_add",
    "i_LIDE_us", "i_SESE_us", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro", "rh_residual", "ri_residual")
  opt <- list()
  for (id in optimizer_ids) {
    m <- fits[[id]]; dat <- fit_data[[id]]
    alt <- rd_fit(paste0(id, "_bfgs"), formula(m), formula(m, component = "disp"), dat,
      if (startsWith(id, "h") || startsWith(id, "rh")) "height" else "increment",
      stage = "optimizer", family = family(m), second_optimizer = TRUE)
    opt[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, alternative_id = paste0(id, "_bfgs"),
      primary_usable = rd_usable(m), alternative_usable = rd_usable(alt),
      absolute_objective_difference = abs(m$fit$objective - alt$fit$objective),
      max_conditional_prediction_difference = max(abs(predict(m, type = "response", re.form = NA) -
        predict(alt, type = "response", re.form = NA))))
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(opt), "optimizer-checks")
  loo <- list()
  for (base_id in c("h_diagonal", "i_full", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro")) {
    endpoint <- if (startsWith(base_id, "h")) "height" else "increment"
    m <- fits[[base_id]]; dat <- fit_data[[base_id]]
    for (site in levels(wide$site)) {
      dd <- droplevels(filter(dat, .data$site != .env$site))
      id <- paste0(base_id, "_omit_", match(site, levels(wide$site)))
      alt <- rd_fit(id, formula(m), formula(m, component = "disp"), dd, endpoint, stage = "leave_site_out", family = family(m))
      if (rd_usable(alt)) {
        z <- rd_means(alt, dd, endpoint, id)
        loo[[id]] <- mutate(rd_contrasts(z, endpoint), omitted_site = site)
      }
    }
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(loo), "leave-one-site-out-contrasts")
}

All 11 full-cohort optimizer checks have usable Hessians and agree within 0.00000002 in objective and 0.000075 in conditional response prediction. The four height omissions preserve a positive redwood GS–HD difference (3.76–5.59 m), while HA–HD ranges from 0.05 to 1.58 m. Joint-model temporal GS–HD contrasts change sign across omissions. Thus the broad size contrast is more stable than the arrangement or differential-slowing interpretation.
Of 16 site-omission fits, 13 satisfy both convergence and Hessian criteria. The temporal-macro candidates encounter singular convergence when Camp Six is omitted for either species and when Waldo South is omitted for redwood; the redwood Camp Six omission also lacks a positive-definite Hessian. Those models remain in the fit register, but their intervals are excluded from the contrast table. We have not weakened convergence checks or dropped those sites. The complete four-site candidates are stable under BFGS, but this three-site instability limits confidence in an elaborate temporal covariance.


Residual behavior and simulation support
We inspect residual location, spread, tails, paired increment association, and macro-level patterns, with 500 unconditional simulations per focal candidate using seed 20261106. These diagnostics include both the Gaussian and Gamma height candidates, the joint and separate temporal-macro increment candidates, and the two residual-tree fits. The simulation count is for diagnostics, not a refitted uncertainty bootstrap. Conditional paired residual correlations are affected by fitted clump effects and must not be read as estimates of the marginal two-period covariance.
The simulation table checks whether data generated by each model resemble the observations. The nonpositive fraction is particularly useful for spotting impossible predicted heights; the diagnostic p-values help identify departures that merit inspection, rather than certify that a model is correct.


Code
if (recompute) {
  diagnostic_ids <- c("h_diagonal", "h_identity", "h_gamma", "i_full", "i_LIDE_macro", "i_SESE_macro", "rh_residual", "ri_residual")
  diagnostic <- grouped <- macro <- paired <- plots <- list()
  for (k in seq_along(diagnostic_ids)) {
    id <- diagnostic_ids[k]; m <- fits[[id]]; mf <- model.frame(m)
    stopifnot(rd_usable(m))
    set.seed(20261106L + k - 1L)
    sims <- simulate(m, nsim = 500L)
    dh <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse = as.matrix(sims), observedResponse = model.response(mf),
      fittedPredictedResponse = rowMeans(as.matrix(sims)), integerResponse = FALSE, seed = 20261106L + k - 1L)
    diagnostic[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, simulations = 500L, seed = 20261106L + k - 1L,
      uniformity_p = testUniformity(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
      dispersion_p = testDispersion(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
      outliers_p = testOutliers(dh, plot = FALSE, type = "bootstrap")$p.value,
      simulated_nonpositive_fraction = mean(as.matrix(sims) <= 0),
      observed_nonpositive_fraction = mean(model.response(mf) <= 0))
    rr <- fit_data[[id]] |> mutate(model_id = id, fitted = as.numeric(predict(m, type = "response")),
      residual = as.numeric(residuals(m, type = "pearson")), scaled_residual = dh$scaledResiduals)
    if (!"spp" %in% names(rr)) rr$spp <- "SESE"
    if (!"period" %in% names(rr)) rr$period <- "year10"
    grouped[[id]] <- rr |> group_by(model_id, spp, treat, period) |>
      summarise(n = n(), mean_residual = mean(residual), sd_residual = sd(residual),
        q025 = quantile(residual, .025), q975 = quantile(residual, .975),
        mean_scaled_residual = mean(scaled_residual), .groups = "drop")
    macro[[id]] <- rr |> group_by(model_id, site, plot, spp, period) |>
      summarise(n = n(), mean_residual = mean(residual), .groups = "drop")
    if ("ht_inc" %in% names(rr)) {
      pairs <- rr |> select(model_id, tree, spp, treat, period, residual) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = residual, names_prefix = "p")
      paired[[id]] <- pairs |> group_by(model_id, spp, treat) |>
        summarise(n_clumps = n(), conditional_residual_correlation = cor(p5, p10), .groups = "drop")
    }
    plots[[id]] <- rr |> select(model_id, fitted, residual, scaled_residual)
  }
  p2_write(bind_rows(diagnostic), "simulation-diagnostics")
  p2_write(bind_rows(grouped), "grouped-residuals")
  p2_write(bind_rows(macro), "macro-residuals")
  p2_write(bind_rows(paired), "paired-residuals")
  diag_plot <- ggplot(bind_rows(plots), aes(fitted, residual)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55") + geom_point(alpha = .35, size = .7) +
    facet_wrap(~model_id, scales = "free", ncol = 2) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    labs(x = "Conditional fitted response (m or m/year)", y = "Conditional Pearson residual",
      title = "RD03 exploratory model diagnostics")
  ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"), diag_plot, width = 9, height = 9, dpi = 160, bg = "white")
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records), "rd03-fit-register")
  writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(p2, "tables/session-info.txt"))
}

The residual plot complements the tables by showing curves, changing spread, or extreme observations that averages can hide. We use it to decide which model assumptions need closer review before accepting a display.


Code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"))









Gaussian(log) year-10 simulations produce 0.47% nonpositive heights, versus 0.66% for the identity link and none for Gamma. Gamma nevertheless has poorer AIC and a uniform-residual diagnostic p-value of 0.0015, so positive support alone does not make it preferable. The separate temporal-macro increment models generate roughly 1.25% nonpositive tanoak and 1.77% nonpositive redwood increments, compared with none observed. Gaussian increments permit negative changes in principle, but this lower-tail mismatch deserves targeted review. The simulation diagnostics do not otherwise flag strong overall dispersion or outlier departures; their nonsignificant p-values do not validate the models. The residual figure also retains the larger positive increment tail. We retain the family/support trade-off for Phase Three rather than claiming that any candidate passes all scientific checks.


Human review summary and Phase Three handoff
Phase Two is complete. I recommend the models below as the starting point for Phase Three; none is yet accepted for the manuscript. We used all 692 recorded clumps, as approved in human review. Each treatment was represented at four sites; the hundreds of clumps are subsamples within those treatment units. Some blocks may have had too few clumps to reach the sampling target, but we have no original roster to confirm that explanation. Our results describe this recorded cohort and cannot establish survival or recruitment across the stand.
The model names identify the response and species: h means year-10 height, i means annualized height change, SESE is redwood, and LIDE is tanoak. Here, height always follows the tallest sprout on a clump at each visit; the tallest stem may change between visits.
Year-10 height: the separate redwood model, h_SESE, estimates that GS clumps were 4.65 m taller than HD clumps on average. Its estimate for HA minus HD is only 0.96 m, with an approximate interval from -0.63 to +2.56 m. The joint model, h_diagonal, gives almost the same two differences: 4.64 and 0.99 m. When we refitted h_diagonal leaving out one site at a time, GS minus HD remained positive, whereas HA minus HD ranged from 0.05 to 1.58 m. Thus GS versus HD is the stronger result to carry forward. We should not yet claim a clear advantage of aggregated retention (HA) over dispersed retention (HD).
Change in growth rate: i_SESE_macro models redwood separately and allows each macro plot to have a different growth rate in each measurement period. It estimates that annual height change was lower in years 5–10 than in years 1–5 by about 0.16, 0.16, 0.06, and 0.12 m/year under GS, LD, HA, and HD, respectively. However, its intervals do not clearly distinguish how much slowing occurred under GS versus HD or HA versus HD. The corresponding tanoak model, i_LIDE_macro, also estimates slowing under every treatment, but each interval includes no change. These two models fit better than i_SESE and i_LIDE, which assume that a macro plot’s contribution stays constant across periods. I recommend carrying i_SESE_macro and i_LIDE_macro forward, because that constant contribution would cancel when comparing periods and leave out variation among treatment units in how growth changed.
There is an important limit to those growth models. Both fit successfully using all four sites and agree under two fitting algorithms. But three of their eight site-omission fits had convergence problems: both species when Camp Six was omitted, and redwood when Waldo South was omitted. Phase Three needs to examine that instability before accepting their uncertainty intervals. We should not remove those sites or treat the failed fits as reliable results.
Residual redwood trees: rh_residual compares year-10 redwood height between clumps with and without a tree left after harvest, allowing for treatment and site. It estimates about 5% greater height with a residual tree, but the interval ranges from about 5% shorter to 16% taller. ri_residual makes the corresponding growth-rate comparison and also leaves both suppression and augmentation plausible. Neither model improves fit enough to justify adding the indicator to the main analysis. I recommend keeping these as secondary exploratory results and leaving residual_rw out of the main treatment models. This comparison uses LD, HA, and HD only: GS has no residual trees. It does not establish that retaining a tree causes either a benefit or a reduction in growth.
Use the following table as the Phase Three decision list: it names the models we recommend carrying forward and the checks still needed before accepting each one. This makes the next analysis choices explicit without treating the current candidates as final selections.








Question
Recommended Phase Three starting models
What to check before acceptance




Year-10 height
Start with h_SESE and h_LIDE: separate Gaussian(log) models with treatment, site, and macro-plot effects. Keep h_diagonal and h_fixed as joint-species comparisons.
Check simulated heights and uncertainty for each separate model. The related h_diagonal model generates about five nonpositive heights per 1,000 simulated measurements. h_gamma avoids this but fits the observed data less well.


Change in growth rate
Start with i_SESE_macro and i_LIDE_macro, which allow different amounts of slowing among treatments and macro plots.
Investigate the failed site-omission fits and calibrate uncertainty. Keep i_full as a comparison: it assumes one macro contribution across periods and shares clump variance across species. i_diagonal also forces equal slowing across treatments within a species.


Residual trees
Keep rh_residual and ri_residual as secondary checks against their matching models without the indicator, rh_base and ri_base.
Report the LD/HA/HD comparison and its uncertainty. Do not add the indicator to the main treatment models or expand the interaction search on this evidence.



For all main comparisons, I recommend averaging the four site predictions equally when reporting treatment means, rather than weighting them by the number of clumps sampled. The current intervals are approximate; Phase Three still needs to assess their reliability with only four sites.
The next analyst should proceed in this order:

Read this summary, the candidate plan, and the numerical evidence above. Checkpoint the Phase Two sources and versioned outputs before further analytical changes. Run python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --inputs-only --protected and python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --task RD03 --domains sprouts --require-models. All 54 fits, including failed site omissions, have ignored RDS files under outputs/sprouts/phase-two/models/; the fit register records their status. Missing fits are prerequisites, not authority to silently refit.
Review the recommended models in the table before making a final selection. For i_SESE_macro and i_LIDE_macro, investigate why some three-site fits fail and explain any simpler model used in response. Retain variation among macro plots in the change between periods. Fit the planned joint-height sensitivity: one model of heights at years 1, 5, and 10, treating the visits as separate ages rather than assuming a straight growth line. Derive both interval changes from that model, so the shared year-5 measurement is handled within one analysis. It has not been fitted in Phase Two. A lognormal height model is also untested; add it only if reviewing simulated low heights and residuals gives a reason to do so. If added, include the likelihood Jacobian for comparison and the correction needed to report arithmetic means.
Review species/treatment/period and macro residual tables and the diagnostic figure, including the negative simulation fractions. Keep the observed-site arithmetic target consistent and do not compare AIC across endpoints or across different row subsets. Cross-species formal contrasts require a joint covariance model or paired hierarchical simulation; separate fits alone do not supply them. Do not expand the residual-tree search merely to find a favorable association.
Assess uncertainty by simulating new datasets from each chosen model and refitting it 2,000 times, using seed 20261116. This is the planned parametric bootstrap; it has not been run. Preserve the 16 macros, species, repeated clumps, observed site blocks, and fitted heterogeneity. Integrate log-link macro effects within every refit so that their variance uncertainty enters arithmetic means. Report failures, boundaries, Monte Carlo endpoint stability, and intervals’ dependence on model assumptions. Use the four predeclared redwood contrasts with Holm adjustment if confirmatory testing is retained; other comparisons stay exploratory. This checks uncertainty under the chosen model’s assumptions; it does not account for uncertainty about which model to choose or bias from how clumps were sampled.
Only after reviewing model adequacy and calibrated contrasts, prepare the proposed size/time figure and caption for acceptance. If treatment-specific temporal evidence remains weak, use an appropriately labeled pooled change or place temporal detail in the supplement. Refresh RD03, then its RT02, M02, and D02 review records from the registry. Those tasks remain queued; no manuscript claim or publication figure is accepted by this phase.

An ordinary render reads the saved tables. -P recompute:true rebuilds the audit, model summaries, predictions, diagnostics, and influence records from saved fits; -P refit:true refits this complete Phase Two sequence. Neither mode executes the unimplemented Phase Three bootstrap or joint-height sensitivity. No thesis environment, input export, package dependency, or RD02 result changed.
Phase Two gives us named models to take forward and a clearer distinction between the results they support. The year-10 GS–HD redwood height difference is consistent across the tested models. HA–HD height differences and differences among treatments in how much growth slowed need more cautious interpretation. Phase Three should now review the recommended models, assess their uncertainty, and prepare a display for acceptance while keeping the conclusions about this recorded clump cohort.
